Ignore the time spent playing. which for some reason is completely misrepresented, possibly due to a bug. I've played countless hours between the PC version and the Xbox 360 port, and I can say, with vindication, that Terraria is not so much a game as it is a petty time-sink.  Terraria was not inspired by Minecraft. It *is* Minecraft - Minecraft as presented in a two-dimensional space and rendered with sprites. Minecraft is intensely popular, so it stands to reason that this game - which doesn't even really attempt to conceal the fact that it's a blatant copy - is unreasonably popular as well. This game is loved by 12 year olds everywhere, and it's already sold its thousands upon thousands of dollars' worth of copies. But for those few of us "traditional" gamers who are left sitting on the fence, wondering if this critically-acclaimed Minecraft-esque "sandbox" might not be so bad after all, take it from me: it's bad. It's very, very bad.  Now, why would I say this while claiming I've played the game for an obscene amount of time? The answer is easy. Games like this are built for the "grind" - they're constructed for the sole purpose of wasting your life to artificially pad their own extreme lack of depth. If I've played this game, say, 72 hours, then I can say without hesitation that 50 of those hours were spent holding down a directional input and the "use item" key, watching my character loop a pickaxe swing animation over and over and over again, and waiting.   Strip out this facet of the game, the whole concept of "mining," and more than half of the experience is moot - the other half is holding the use item key and bumping yourself into barely-animating "monsters," hoping to "out-DPS" them with your better numbers before they do the same to you. No wonder today's "gamers" are so enamored with this one. It requires extremely little thought. In lieu of tired-old RPG stat-based mechanics, we have tired, old RPG gear-based number mechanics. The imperative is to grind enough randomly-distributed materials to get palette swapped items with bigger numbers. That's it.  The game wishes to appeal to our innate love for exploration, which is a noble goal, but ultimately it fails in execution. The worlds are randomly generated, but this merely boils down to "hidden rooms with treasure chests can be here, here, or HERE." No elaborate, sprawling underground ruins, no crumbling catacombs, no abandoned villages: just a bunch of differently-colored blocks of dirt with scattered structures that serve as an excuse to hold candy-bag treasure chests. Sometimes, the accessories found in these chests hint at fun, and the game toys with the concept of breaking its own rules with double-jumps, rocket boots, and other gravity-defying trinkets, but the game never transcends its one-button aspirations.  A major flaw rests in the core design of the game. The two primary difficulties are both...wrong. The easiest makes it so that you lose only money on death, which was of only minimal use to begin with. With no other penalty for dying, many players just dump their money in a chest, go grind up a bunch of stuff, then throw themselves into the lava to teleport back home, which neuters the game completely and strips it of any challenge or depth. Then the "mediumcore" mode sees you drop absolutely everything on death, which gives failure the necessary gravitas, but at the same time it makes the game's constant, endless enemy spawns and cheap one-hit deaths stand out as the extreme flaws that they are. Technically the "you're dead forever" hardcore mode doesn't really count, because your progress is tied to your gear anyway, not your character. If you lose your gear, it's a long, slow trek back to where you were, which often proves next to impossible without help as your mobility is savaged without all those above mentioned accessories, and your character is mauled to death by the weakest of enemies regardless of your own experience with the game. As a straight numbers experience, without your gear, you are essentially dead meat trying to get your stuff back.  For example, have fun getting killed over and over again by the "King Slime," a boss that can spawn at random, who will instantly teleport right on top of you and one-shot your freshly respawned, equipment-less character. That's right, he teleports right on top of you, and your starting character is too slow to do anything about it. Either de-log from the game, and lose all of your dropped stuff forever, or tough it out and wait until the boss despawns thirty minutes later. What's not to love about watching your character die and respawn endlessly for a half an hour? Stuff like this shows that the devs really don't bother to analyze some of their ideas at length before just implementing them into the game.  With nothing bridging the gap between "so easy the entire experience is easily-abused and utterly moot" and "so frustrating that this game is not worth the increase in blood pressure," I cannot in good faith recommend it.  On the positive side, the game is very, very good looking. Its deceptively simple sprite art is charming, and the lighting is quite good, especially when outdoors and in the rain. And it's always thrilling to tap a water reservoir and watch a cascade go spilling down a shaft into the caverns below. Occasionally finding a new item that actually changes the way your character interacts with the world is a momentary thrill that fades when you go back to mining the same old dirt tiles five minutes later, in the exact same way you've been doing it for the past 10 hours or so.  It should be mentioned before closing that the game's interface is terrible on the PC version, and, inexplicably, the console version's is infinitely superior. One would think the opposite should be true for this sort of game. Accessing, organzing, and swapping your items is a massive pain and almost impossible to do properly under stress. The keyboard controls for movement are horrible and suffer from noticeable lag - acrobatic feats with the grappling hook, easy enough to pull off with some practice on the console, are next to impossible on the PC version. Ranged weapons are a nightmare to aim, as the best you can do is to point in the general direction of your target - aiming with the regular cursor - and click. And again - that grappling hook! Same mechanic - point in the general direction and click, and hope the game registers the direction properly.  Way too many flaws, way too little effort to elevate itself beyond its Minecraft-aping roots. I would recommend it for its occasional thrills of sort-of-discovey, but only at a deep discount. Even at its modest initial asking price of $10,  it's too expensive for a game in which the majority of your time is, inevitably, spent hammering away at rock walls. Which is what you're going to feel like doing with your head in real life with every one of this game's abundant flaws and cheap deaths.

I got Civilization V back when it was freshly released, and like many players I was extremly unhappy with the way Civ V was a massive step back from Civ IV. A lot of people say that the DLC makes Civ 5 fun again, but you can't simply release a broken game and then sell DLC to make it what it should have been from the start. That kind of practice just leaves a sour taste in your fans' mouths.  I bought Civilization I on release, and every other version since. Civ V is the first one that I can't even begin to enjoy. It's a massive step backwards. It's basically no longer Civilization, but some weird war game without any of the depth that made all the previous versions fun to play and saw the series progress with each iteration. If anything, Civ V is kinda like Civ I in that it essentially removes all the additions to the series in between.   The big difference is that Civ I was actually fun to play and gave you the feeling of building a "Civilization to stand the test of time". This is a monstrosity not worthy of the name. I definitely won't be purchasing Civ VI in blind faith - and I never thought that I'd say that about a Civ game!   Now a lot of people are saying the same thing about Civ VI - severely lacking in many respects and not a patch on Civ V; buy Civ V instead. I would urge you to not buy Civ V either. It's quite clear that this is Firaxis' preferred approach to releasing games, and you should not be supporting a company like that.

Oh wait they've put that core mechanic into a DLC food is stilll required for growth, but Housing caps your max size throughout the tech tree, so there's less reason to expend energy building a good city.  most city buildings are locked behind districts, which override, replace and occupy space for improvements (although tile improvements are still technically in the game,  all your work improving tiles early-game will be negated when you need those best tiles for districts). Religion is actually a little better; it's basically a parallel battle system that mostly ignores the rest of the game 	so you can fight other civs without bothering with diplomacy. Another great driving simulation from SCS.  If you've played Euro Truck Simulator 2, then you know what you're getting, just with different scenery, different trucks, and a bit less content right now.  More content will arrive with time.  If ETS 2 is anything to go by, some of it will be free, some of it will be paid DLC.  Even with the current amount of content (California, Arizona, Nevada) there is still a good bit of ground to cover and plenty fun to be had.  ETS 2 was that game that started out being a joke around the gaming community, because of the fact that there are a billion "simulator" games out there and 98% of them are garbage.  Then some people actually played ETS 2 and found out, wait a minute, this game is actually good.  Then the news spread and it stopped being a joke and people caught on to the fact that it's just plain a good game.  ATS follows the groundwork that ETS 2 set and takes the fun across the Atlantic to North America.  The game does a good job of simulating a scaled down west coast US.  The driving model is pretty faithful to reality, though now 100% accurate.  Still, it's far from arcadey and big rigs feels and handle like you would expect them to had you ever driven, or even ridden in one before.  The game plays well on a gamepad, but really shines if you have a proper wheel and pedal setup.  I've never tried it with VR, but I imagin it's pretty spectacular if you couple VR with wheel & pedal for a fully immersive experience.  I've been asked many times what the hook for a game like this is.  Why would you want to drive a big rig around and haul cargo back and forth?  That sounds really mundane.  It is, but it's also really relaxing.  Sometimes you need to take a break from shooting things and chopping monsters with a sword and just play something chill and relaxing.  Rolling in a big rig, listening to some good tunes, and watching the open road roll by fits the bill nicely.

This is not a bad game. The concept is original and, when the stars align, fun. What irritates me is the whole character progression system, un-fun options being the best options, and the infrequency of bug fixes.  Personally, I think this game would have been better without the "growing characters". Every survivor is the same starting out, you have to spend hours upon hours in-game to get anything that makes them unique. New players have no tools outside of fundamental gameplay that lets them contribute meaningfully.  Killers, on the other hand, can either be a joke or a terror, based entirely on how much time the player has invested.  As far as I have been able to tell, camping a survivor as the killer is your best strategy, especially as the game's best killer, Trapper. Survivors have no way of offensively threatening the Killer or communicating with random players, so incoming help usually does little but change who's dying. Conversely, the best strategy for a survivor is to leave the dying player alone due to the above. There is no being a hero unless your killer also wants to have fun.  The dev team doesn't seem particularly interested in fixing the multitude of bugs plaguing DbD, many of which have no reason to exist. One example springs to mind, where a killer's facial model will clip into first person view, interfering with vision based on which killer is dealing with it. This has been an issue for months.  If you must get this, find it on sale. Otherwise, look elsewhere until this gets cleaned up.

Upfront, you can tell the game is made with great care. The art is lovingly drawn, the designs are made with care for detail, the soundtrack is atmospheric.  Yet, three hours in, I decided to quit. I quit because the game wasn't fun for me. There's a lot of reasons to it, but most of all, it's because I do not like how it plays - or to be more precise, how it punishes playing the game.  I like exploration. It's a major appeal to most games, and admittedly, Hollow Knight has a lot to explore and see. Traversing the map, however, is not enjoyable. Many, many rooms have a drawn-out vertical layout, with enemies and acid pits strewn around for good measure. Due to how the controls work, jumping down may leave you with no option to course correct, landing you in one or another damage source. Which is the next point: I strongly dislike the controls. Attacking does not grant you invincibility frames. It also pushes you back. This leads to some very unintuitive gameplay where you more often than not push yourself away from one enemy only to fall into a spike trap.  In case you think there's gonna be a double-jump to save you, you are mistaken. You actually can heal yourself, but for some unimaginable reason, healing takes a certain amount of time, consuming its necessary resource regardless of whether or not you finish the heal. I.e. you press the button for 0.95s instead of 1s.   My biggest gripe, however, is with the feeling of accomplishment. In this case, the lack thereof: The currency of the game is called Geo, you collect it, and spent it in the town or various shops. Should you die during your descent, you lose all your Geo and a spirit appears in the room you died - kill it, and you get it all back. Should you die before that, the ghost - and your Geo, - disappears. Some people will say that at the end of the game you have so much Geo and nothing to spent it on, which might be the case, but that only highlights the flaw, not invalidates it. The beginning of the game has you run around basically butt-naked, with no map, no marker, no light, or anything. You actually have to [i]buy[/i] individual markers for resting points, trams, etc. Losing your Geo at the start of the game stings twice - you're just learning the ropes, and while trying to do so, the game robs you of all you have to show for your effort. And that's the thing, outside of bosses, who drop seals, none of your equipment drops outside of shops (at least not up to where I played).  The entire early game seems to be comprised of try - fail - repeat, with no sense that you are advancing in a meaningful way. You don't even get any new skill until like two hours into the game. [i]And it's a shitty attack spell that uses the same resource you use to heal.[/i]  About 3 hours in, there's no story to speak of. There are some "lore" tidbits that you get for inspecting some statues (which you can [i]very[/i] easily miss) and it's rather underwhelming.   People who enjoy steep learning curves and being challenged for the sake of being challenged might enjoy this, but I play games to have fun or be entertained, and Hollow Knight does neither for me.

I both love an hate this game.   It has its good bits, and they are truly inspired. This really puts the 'grand' into grand strategy. The scale and ambition of this game are incredible. With the whole globe to play across, a lenghty timeline (AD1444 to 1821) that can be played as fast or slow as you like, a jaw dropping number of nations to play as, and a good attempt at historical accuracy, EU4 should be one of the best strategy games ever concieved. At first glance it really is something special, and the first couple of times I played, it was hard not to be blown away by the sheer scope of things.  But with the rise comes a fall, and that awesome feeling of grandure that initially infects you when you are hurled onto this vast, intricate medieval world stage is quickly sullied when you discover just how truly broken things are. Many complain that vanilla is nigh-on unplayable, something Paradox remedied - not with patches and updates - but with a deluge of paid DLC that has flooded the sidelines of this game with endless 'immersion packs' that are mediocre at best and cancerous at worst. To release a sizable DLC that adds some new mechanics to a select few nations THEN release ridiculously priced 'content pack' alongside it (containing a few skins for a sprinkling troops that are usually too small to see properly anyway and an extra tune for the soundtrack) is the worst form of greed going. that 'content' could and should have been relased with the immersion pack. A DLC that, at full price, will set you back on avergage £10-£15. Paradox are just adding to the bad name game devs are making for themselves in this dark age of DLC crap.  Add to that some questionable mechanics (most notable of which is the infamously infuraiting dice system that makes a mockery of the strategy element and strips away any kind of advantage even the best laid plans might have given) and after a while it seems you're more of a spectator waiting for dumb-as-fuck allies to do most of the work because your own armies were wiped out due to a series of unfortunate rolls of Yahtzee rather than a series of actual battles.  Most enemy armies and fleets will march away at the first sign of an engagement and will lead you on a grand tour of europe, AI will produce better generals and rulers, your good heirs with great stats will die in hunting accidents while useless monarchs that act like an anchor for you progress live to the ripe old age of 75. Those heirs do like to hunt! The main bulk of your 20k stack lands in enemy territory via transport, only to be wiped out by a force half its size because your general stayed behind with the 2k stack that didn't fit on the boats.   This list goes on.  It was great while it lasted, but with even more DLC on the horizon, and a recent game where France happily steam-rolled through an alliance of four strong nations and their allies that attacked her from all sides (BTW, thanks to Austria for marching a 40k stack straight past France where it was most needed to go and lay siege somewhere in Portugual). Sad as it may sound (and because people on forums will tell everyone they just have conformation bias) I actually counted up the dice rolls that eventually broke my patience. 16 winning rolls to 59 losing, with 5 draws. Too much (bad) luck involved to bother with anymore.  The game is so grand and intricate, and the code for such a venture must be impossibly difficult, but when things like that happen time and time again, it all begins to stack up and grate on you. As such my own war exhaustion has finally caught up with me and reached its limit.  If you love grand strategy and are feeling flush enough to get the expansion DLCs (Rights of Man, Art of War, and Common Sense are the absoulte must haves) then pick it up. It's an experience like no other, I had some fun with it, and sunk a fair few hours in, but eventually the randomness and the sheer stupidity of some of the mechanics just withered my patience away.  Make sure you pick everything up while it's 50-75% off. That's the best way to get a fair deal.  Oh, and pray like burggery to those dice gods!

[h1]Insufferable, Sheer Stupidity. Just Don't.[/h1]  Allow me to start by saying that I adore story-heavy games. Love them to death.   After reading rave reviews about this game's amazing, tear-inducing plotline, I decided to give it a try.   It failed to suck me in at first, but I nonetheless stuck with it through the slow, horrendous gameplay, and several exceedingly weird scenes (that one zombie scene comes to mind...), in hopes of eventually getting overwheled by an astounding twist or reveal in the story, one way or another.   But no such thing happened.   Instead, I was smacked in the face by the game's excuse of a plotline, tear-inducing in all its right, but not at all through emotional depth or significance, but from its sheer incompetency in being able to make sense, much less entertain.   Perhaps I'm too critical, seeing to how my opinion is vastly different from many of the others who've played this game and fell in love with it, but the way I see it, "To The Moon" is a complete waste of time.   The game's storyline is convoluted, shallow, and nonsensical at best, and the "plot twist" (if it even merits that title), sorry to say, consists of nothing more than sheer STUPIDITY. Paired with it's lazy gameplay mechanics, this game did nothing but frustrate and annoy me the whole way through.   Although I got it on sale for only a dollar or so, I still feel cheated. I'm never getting those hours of my life back.  Do yourself a favor, and don't bother with this game. Just don't.

Man, I *really* want to like this game. After all, I have ~50 hrs in it for a reason.  The art and sound direction does a great job at creating a dark, gloomy mood that can still be frightening. The quirk and stress mechanics are great ideas to make the game more difficult/interesting in a way that is still (supposed to be) manageable. There are enough good character classes that there are many different usable party configurations.  But I gotta say, this game just isn't fun.  I can't count how many times that, for no identifiable reason, all the enemies in a battle focused on one party member (sometimes for a few turns in a row) which would end up nearly killing them, giving them a mental breakdown, or both. Some of the classes are by my estimation either basically useless (ex.: antiquarian) or only good as support which is not an archetype that works well later (vestal). All attacks only work in certain positions in battle, which can make party selection and combat a pain if you don't want to worry about moving party members around mid-battle (which takes up their turn I think, I might be wrong there). Sometimes characters doing stress-relief activities will take an extra day doing them; I quit my last run when half of my 9-man party did this all at once. Some negative quirks aren't too bad, but there are some that are atrocious (plus there are diseases, which are almost always pretty bad), which can cost quite a bit to remove and even more if you don't remove them quickly and they get "severe" (i.e they won't be rotated out if the character gets a new negative quirk but all the slots are filled).  Because of all the above, it can be really easy to get knocked down into a bad position early and either have to grind to get back to neutral or just quit. I'd go as far to say that it's almost likely this will happen on any given run, because more of my half-dozen or so runs ended this way.  You could probably overlook these things and still enjoy the game, if you're really into the grindy masochism involved in games like this - years ago, I did just that, had several characters with maxed out equipment and levels, and had the final level unlocked. They all died, which isn't that upsetting - I was just happy to make it that far anyway. But in light of the above, I can't help but feel like the frustrating slog involved to get back to that point isn't worth it just to probably die again.

The overall balance seems extremely poor; some dungeons you will receive 50% the number of enemies, and they will all be of an easy type and other dugeons will have twice as many enemies and each fight will decimate your party.  Add in the unavoidable RNG (you can be unlucky with what hero types are available, giving you an unfeasable party configuration leading to certain failure) and this game is just not worth the price of admission.  I hope they refine it, because I feel like this could be a really good game.  One last thing; many people are saying the root problem is that you have to learn the game.  Some of my favorite games are the Souls games which are difficult, but once your endure and learn the mechanics you become powerful.  This is not that scenario; the Souls games are tough but fair.  This game's reliance on RNG outcomes yields and experience which just is not fair.

Did I enjoy playing it?  Immensely.  Do I like it after I played it?  Mostly.  Would I recommend you play it too?  Yeah, probably.  Is it a Great Game?  Ahhhh....no.  The world-concept is brilliantly executed.  The story is thick enough on top of the gameplay that you 'feel' for the situation and people in it.  I cannot recommend the feel of the game highly enough!  The interface and look go to reinforce this too, so really great job guys.  However under this all, the gameplay is just a rudimentary and simple city builder.  Get people.  House people.  Get coal.  Stay warm.  Get other stuff.  Rinse, repeat.  There is zero here that hasn't been done a million times in a city builder.    What disappointed me was the early game 'timing' of the random stuff, the duplication/waste in the tech tree, and the unwarned and sudden drop-off at the end.    The 'timing' issue is the only hazard against a perfectly functioning (boring) city for the main part of the game.  For example, you have a request to heat houses, but if that coincides with a cold weather drop, then you are (to put it simply) stuffed.  At a later point, you will encounter a fractious faction.  If that coincides with you not having any hope-generating stuff to do, then you are (to put it simply) stuffed again.  While a second play attempt can leverage the knowledge of your first play through, to do so is to break the immersion barrier entirely, which is such a critical aspect to this game to make it something other than a very basic city builder.  On the other hand, if you just happen to get the timing right, then your experience is back to 'vanilla city builder'.  There really is no sweet spot here, and that's a strategic weakness in the game design that can dictate your fun/boredom/annoyance more than any other factor.  The duplicate tech tree is just a lazy design decision.  There are multiple answers to the heat/resource issues at hand, and they should be like the Policy tree - pick one to the exclusion of others.  Instead, you can go down several like-paths - which will set you up for massive wastage.  Also some trees are brute-force better than others.  Again, experience of a first play through would have resolved this, but I wonder why the design does not leverage the excellent exclusion mechanism that was so carefully introduced already?  Last, the ending. There is no 'lead up' that indicates the sorts of things you will need.  And in my play there was totally insufficient time to attend to the chasm.  Maybe the 'triggers' in my game were encountered in an inauspicious order.  Maybe I just chose unwisely, or unluckily.  Regardless of how I got there, the lead-up to the end game came as a total disappointment in that I had not 'guessed' what I might need in future.  Is it a great game?  No, the flaws hold it back.  It needs some work on the complexity of the play to make it much more than a single-direction city building sim, and some more pressure in terms of getting you directed towards your longer term goals.  The multiple tech trees need to be refined down to meaninful choices, not avoidance of options.  The cost of certain buildings is absurd.  So, do I recommend it.  If you buy it, you will guaranteed get a good number of hours out of it which will be really interesting and fun.  But you may end up hating it.  And for that reason, I cannot recommend it.

I remember finding this game 5 years ago and was intrigued, but then decided to not get it because reviews said the game was buggy. Well time passed and we met again, now released. I jumped on it immidiately and played through the night.  I am Mu the Wanderer, I arrived at a stranded town called "The Hub", with only an iron bar and a few Cats (Kenshi's currency) to my name. First thing I did was leaving the town to explore the vicinity but as I took a few steps out of the game, I was greeted by a group of armed men in rags, demanding all the food I have. I told them I had none, which then they suddenly attacked. I fought back, like how I did in other RPGs but then I realized I'm the only one getting hit. With death near, I used all that's left to run into town, which then the guards briefly dismissed the group of bandits. After bandaging my wounds, I looted the dying bandits, one afer another. Then started my job as a scavenger.   After that, I go outside towns everyday, looking for bandits. When they got their eyes on me, I run back to town and let the guards do the fighting. I was too weak to fight them, I tried and almost died so now I just run. Though, the guards doesn't finish them off so I practiced swordplay on the crippled bandits, who were crawling for their lives. One after another, bandits to slave traders, I lured them into town and looted their dying bodies. The business is lucrative, the Cats is good, good enough that I bought a small shack in town on my 3rd day, then recruited a weakling to be "bait", why get hurt when someone else can do it for you?  It's now the 8th day, I have bought the biggest house in town as well as recruited another bait. Less dead bandits at The Hub's doorsteps now, they are getting smarter. Many stop giving chase into towns or hunting near The Hub so the baits now have crossbows to attack first. I'm not sure if I will ever leave The Hub but I don't see any reasons to. For now, I am Mu, a Scavenger, a weakling, a runner, a coward and the richest man of The Hub, and that makes it all okay.  So, if you're thinking if this game is for you. Here's some questions that might help:  - Do you like Mount & Blade: Warband?  - Do you enjoy a game where there is no big goal, no end game, no ending? Where you are free to do what you want, go where you want without any objective binding you? - Are you okay with not being babysit from the beginning? Where you are a scrappy weakling that loses to goats? - Are you okay with playing a game that have pretty crappy graphics?   Well if most of the answers are "Yes", then you should try it.   What I like about Kenshi: - The world is vast, it would take you potentially months to explore all of it. - The freedom in gameplay to allow you to be whatever you want, but you have to work for it.  - The stat grows by what you do, you can carry more if you always lug heavy gears around, you fight better with a weapon the more you use it. You run faster the more you move. There's no shortcut.  - The combat system is diverse, you have many weapon choices as well as potential strategies.  - There's just so much more I rather not say, besides from what I wrote below, I like everything else.   What I don't like about Kenshi: - The graphics is very outdated, this is not a AAA game as you can probably see.  - The price, I disagree with $29.99. Yes, for some people as well as me, $30 is worth it for this game but then, it can be a bit steep for people to give it a chance , especially when the screenshots/videos looks worse than many games from 2010. I would say $20 is the sweet spot and many would disagreed with me but my point stands, I want people to try this game and $30 might not be a good hook.  Would I recommend this game? Certainly, it can be hundred hours of gameplay

There are barely any combats in this game. All you do is walk your 3 man executioner line(potentially actually hiding or using high ground against tougher enemies) initiate combat and shoot for stealth kill. Rinse and repeat that every single area for 95% of enemies in the game. For the boss or some special case you will stun the enemy and kill them within 2 turns. It was okay for first couple areas till you realize that is all the game has to offer in terms of gameplay. Game was balanced completely around the stealth kills. Normal weapons might as well not even exist if you play on hardest difficulty. The hit chance was made too simple 25/50/75/100 % chance so you can always get that 100% which took even the slightest of excitement away. This game had a lot of potential but their piss poor balancing is what killed it to me. Incredibly monotonous experience to play. The game gives about 15h playtime if you scrounge every area fully.

[i]tl;dr[/i]: If you don't like idle games then you probably won't enjoy Farm Together.  As soon as you start playing the game it becomes obvious in only a matter of minutes that it's just another idle game with no replayability value. I guess it could be considered a "semi-idle" game if that could be a thing, since you're not exactly standing still all the time, but ultimately you [b]are[/b] just waiting for numbers to go up. The only difference from this idle game to the "traditional" ones is that instead of it being in a 2D plane with a bunch of buttons and progress bars on your screen, this one is 3D and you have to walk to each button, metaphorically speaking.  Basically you plant a crop, you wait for it to grow, you sell your crops, you get the money, you plant more crops, rinse and repeat. There's also in-game quests and steam achievement to give people a sense of completion when they stare at their screen for hours on end waiting for virtual lettuce to grow. People might attempt at an argument by saying that there's more things to do instead of waiting for plants to grow such as feeding barnyard animals, fishing, or even letting your game run in the background while you do something else at a website or real life... but that is the exact definition of what an idle game is. If you're not waiting for item A to be collectable, you're instead waiting for item B to be collectable, simple as that.  There's not much to this game other than being a cutesy idle farming simulator, and you can talk with other people online too I guess? My point is if you're not into idle games, then you probably won't enjoy this game. You can still buy it if you feel like supporting the developers since they made great games in the past, but at that point you might as well buy their previous games instead.

app_name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps
representative_review: 【含剧透】我今天就是要喷Moon工作室和Ori续作剧情  Ori是我为数不多预购期间直接买了两份游戏（一份30美元的steam版和一份50美元在amazon预购的实体典藏版），直到我通关了Ori第二部后我对游戏甚至是整个工作室的负面评价拉满。  以下都是我的个人观点，觉得有问题欢迎讨论！  整个游戏的剧情基本上可以用一塌糊涂来形容，再加上那个毫无逻辑纯粹是恶心人的结局，我都怀疑是不是编剧在报复社会？ 先说结局的大牺牲（不要说什么Ori没死只是变成了树，官方英文版原话用的单词就是sacrifice），我不是不能接受大牺牲的结局，但是大牺牲需要合理的过度和前提，要必须让玩家认同主角确实应该牺牲自己，然而我完全没有看到。Ori的大牺牲无非就是两个目的，一个是拯救朋友库，一个是拯救尼温大陆。关于拯救库，我先问问大家第一部黑子的那些孩子是怎么死的？不就是因为猫头鹰是黑暗系生物与光明系不互容被精灵树的光照死的？怎么到了第二部黑暗系猫头鹰不仅不怕光，而且还能被光治愈翅膀甚至复活？官方吃书？你要是这么个设定还有个毛线的第一部黑子复仇记？好，先不说设定问题，就说Ori的光芒可以救活库，那么这个故事是不是应该讲Ori和库的成长与羁绊，让玩家对Ori和库产生深厚的感情，然后玩家认可牺牲Ori来拯救库。而游戏是怎么讲的呢？开场暴风雨失散，再次见面没过几分钟库直接躺尸到大结局。就算第一部因为黑子的故事让玩家对黑子的孩子库有感情和共鸣，但这也没有让我觉得非牺牲Ori不可，我全程的感受是--因为Ori想救库，所以我想帮Ori救库，但不是我自己想救。也许Ori对库的羁绊深不可测，但是我作为一个玩家除了开头以外没有看到一秒钟的剧情。 咱们再说第二点关于拯救尼温大陆。有多少人在前一半游戏，甚至结局之前认为这是一个Ori和库回家，顺道帮一下尼温大陆的故事？肯定不止我一个吧。Ori和这个尼温大陆一毛钱的关系都没有，要不是库开头瞎飞，这片大陆永远都不会出现在Ori的世界中。在整个游戏中Ori就tm的是一个工具人，全程就是接任务，帮这个，接任务，帮那个。这片大陆没有让我产生一点感情，凭什么让Ori牺牲自己来拯救这片的大陆？这就好比你邻居的家族要得了病要亡了，要用你的命去救他们，你甚至之前都不认识这个邻居，凭什么要我去救？尤其是最后Seir对Ori说的话，还什么命中注定？简直就是道德绑架。还有人说这个结局是升华，真要是升华Ori就应该回到自己的尼泊尔大陆等家里老树老死再牺牲自己来继承。邻居有难我可以帮忙，甚至可以无偿，但是不代表我必须要把自己搭进去。整个游戏，整个尼温大陆从头到尾都在向Ori不停地索取，有让Ori感受到哪怕一点点的家的感觉吗？ 最后再说一个很让我反感的剧情，那就是大boss鸟史雷克。孤儿史雷克因为从小畸形被猫头鹰族敌视，成长过程中堕入黑暗。本来我觉得史雷克的故事应该会很精彩，悲惨的过去应该会有一个救赎或者解脱的结局，结果官方整了一个因为打架打输了回窝里憋屈等死？这tm的是什么故事？这妥妥的就是一个负能量故事，没有救赎没有解脱，我甚至在最后boss战的时候都觉得是莫名其妙的，这场战斗的存在意义是什么？第一部最后的逃脱有着明显的感情冲突，黑子因为憎恨光于是追杀Ori和Sein。而第二部简直莫名其妙，包括沙虫和那个黑暗触手怪，全是凑数的工具人boss。 我相信玩过第一部的人对Ori的感情很深，如果官方想让我认可这个必须牺牲Ori的结局那就要用等价的情感来换，比如让玩家真正爱上这片片大陆和这里的npc，然而整个游戏玩完除了boss鸟史雷克，别的角色我连名字都没有印象，甚至任务道具和隐藏点都比他们给我留下的印象深，然后一代的老角色全体无剧情。在这种没有意义的故事发展下，这个结局简直和喂屎没有区别。整个故事毫无逻辑，就像是写了一个故事的开头，又写了另一个故事的结局，然后中间随便拼凑一下接起来。游戏剧情做成这样不知道是编剧故意还是无能，总之我想说白瞎了这么好美术，音乐，关卡设计。甚至那些恶心人的bug都没有动摇我对这款游戏的喜爱，但是这个失望透顶的剧情，steam差评收好！除非之后官方出决定版或dlc能改结局，或者把中间的故事全部重写让我真正的产生对这片大陆的感情，认可牺牲的结局，否则永远差评！

app_name: Ori and the Will of the Wisps
representative_review: I was disappointed. And i am disappointed that i was disappointed, because this is objectively a good game. Beautiful graphics, tight controls, and satisfying platforming, and additions that it makes sense to add to a second game? That sounds great! On paper. But when i boot it up, and just want to stop playing it after an hour, i cannot with good conscience give it a positive score. And it's not like i dislike these types of games. Prior to buying this, i 100% Ori and the blind forest ON HARD, and loved it! Could not wait to play this game afterwards! But as you will hear... (very mild spoilers ahead)  Lets start with the good stuff:  The graphics: 10/10 absolutely amazing. Smooth animation, gorgeous backgrounds, and overall excellent.   The controls: 9/10 Does what you want, when you want it. a controller is recommended, but not necessary.    Now the meh:  The sountrack. it is [i]fiiine[/i] but none of the tracks really stuck out. and yes, i havent played this game that much, but when crossing areas, none of the music really popped out and made a difference to the mood.   And at last, the bad, which more or less ruined it for me.  The RPG element. I don't understant why they needed it for this game. I loved the story and charachters of the previous game, as it kept the story simple to understand and intimate.  Now, with side characters and merchant with the side quests which they bring, it just makes the thing you do more like a checkbox you tick of, rather than the things you actually want to do, or follow a consistent story.   And the combat, the thing that i like the least about this game. In the previous game, enemies were more an extra challenge to add to the platforming, and combat was simple. Avoid attacks and press attack. nothing special, but it worked, as it was more an addition to the excellent platforming.   now it has become a main part of the game. and i hate it. Sure, you get a bunch of new moves, attacks and combos to do, but it isnt [i] fun [/i]. I feel it only disturbs the progression of the otherwise great platforming. closely related is a part of the upgrade system. In the last game it was simple and enjoyable to feel getting progressively better moves all through the game, but now it is more like "oh, which move do i want to switch out with the new one" or not bothering with it at all.   i will still try to play it some more, and update this if i feel like my opinion has changed.

Wow, I was pleasantly surprised, this game was actually pretty good! It is definitely lacking the polish of a AAA release, is occasionally clunky and flawed, but overall it's great.  Narrative is usually the most important factor in a game for me, and Vampyr delivers. It's well-written, and manages to take itself very seriously without coming off as cheesy. Most characters are interesting and nuanced, and the hint system is pretty cool. Side content is good and integrates seamlessly with the main narrative.  The game world is smaller than it initially appears, but good level design make it seem big during initial exploration, but mostly painless for backtracking (which you'll do a lot of). On Normal Difficulty combat is challenging but fair, and while a tad simplistic is fun and easy to get the hang of. Boss fights are generally pretty good, and there's a few memorable ones.  The OST while not amazing is pretty good, so not much to go over on that front.  In terms of graphics and art direction the game looks pretty, but suffers with the materials work. Some of the materials are noticeably low-res, which is disappointing. Shaders are excellent though, and the game makes ample use of Unreal Engine's visual effects.  So overall, definitely worth picking up in a bundle or on sale. A solid 8/10 game.

I'll start off by saying that I've played a lot of CRPGs -- both the classics and the more modern variants.  Among the more recent titles like Tyranny, PoE1, and Divinity Original Sin 2, this game just feels...okay.  It's not terrible, but it's also not great either.  So I probably wouldn't reccomend it.  On the positive side, the game looks good and runs relatively bug free (at least for me).  Most of the little technical issues I noticed will probably be ironed out in patches.  The changes to the skill and leveling system also made the game mechanics simpler, but still retained a decent amount of depth.  The world felt large (maybe even daunting at first) and there is a lot of stuff to do if you are willing to explore.  In terms of downsides, at the top of the list is the story.  It's just bad -- like Mass Effect 3 level bad.  The entire main quest line felt abrupt, poorly explained, and player choice didn't seem to make any difference in the end.  There was a lot of potential there, but it felt like it was squandered.  This same problem carries over to the side characters.  They feel flat, I didn't care about them, and their side quests were extremely short.  In terms of the other quests, there is a lot of content in the game, but what's there feels a little shallow compared to other games of its type -- even compared to PoE 1.  If you don't play for story, then you play for combat right?  What's here is pretty fun at first.  Yet the game is just too easy (even with level scaling and playing on a higher or the max difficulty).  On my second playthrough, I beat the entire game with only two characters on the max difficulty with level scaling...  Some weapons also seem terribly balanced to the point of breaking combat.  Like the unique ice bow you pick up near Neketaka (six attacks per shot on crit?).  This reduces loadout variation and makes the combat feel much more shallow than it could have been.  Finally, I just want to say that the ship-to-ship combat was terrible.  I'm not sure what the thought behind the text-based ship combat prompt was, but it seems silly.  In many engagements, it is often easier and preferable to simply charge the enemy ship head on, ram them, and then kill the crew.  This is just easier and provides better loot (which begs the question of why it's there in the first place).  It feels like the ship combat and the extremely simple "ship management" system could have just been removed and combat could have just initiated when two ships collide.  Then that time/money could have been devoted to the story/writing.  There is almost no point to upgrading your ship and your crew makes very little difference -- because, again, the actual combat is extremely easy.  Summary:  It's an okay game.  You will probably get your money's worth out of it.  But, for me, it doesn't really measure up to either its forerunners or its current competitors.

I have some unpopular opinions.  My review is at 1.9 hours because [i]that is my absolute limit for stomaching this game[/i].  DISCLAIMER: I am no stranger to repetative, difficult, or grindy games. I grew up with, and still play, the NES. That being said....  PROS: • A creepy storyline that grips you at first • Randomly generated levels & items promotes continuing/replay • Character, enemy, and boss designs are clever and well done • The music is pretty good  CONS: • Game boasts difficulty, but the difficulty actually stems from clunky controls, poor weapon design, and bad hit box locations. • You are not told what items [i]actually do[/i], so you need to alt+tab and refer to an external resource to find out. • Repetative. One life. You die once and you start all over losing all items and progress.  This isn't usually a problem with other games, but here I felt like I was working towards [i]nothing[/i]. It's just not worth the boring grind when all you get is a picture of the stuff you previously found put into a log. *yawn* • Sorry, but I have to mention it. The levels are so ugly. In all honesty; its poop brown. Poop everywhere! Blood, sweat, and poopy tears! The game starts out interesting with a wacko mother, but then you are forced naked into a bloody poop infested dungeon? Seriously? I'm not that interested in finding out why the poop is so important to this little boy's story.  CONCLUSION: I do not recommend this game for it's flawed controls, poor design, and ugly repetitive gameplay.  I'd rather just read the storyline on wikipedia, watch the endings on youtube, and [i]then[/i] go play some original Zelda (good gameplay), Tales of the Maj'eyal (a true roguelike), or Dark Souls (repetitive grind with difficulty relying on actual skill).

Torment: Tides of Numenera seriously needs better reviews. It's a great game. Probably it's in the blood if you grew up on isometric rpg's of the 90-ies (and I know there are many people out there, who did), but I love every aspect of the game, from art to dialogs and lore.  The world of Numenera is very distinct, outstanding, both visually and narratively - a lot of weird things are going on. It provokes exploration and thought.  And the game is heavy on those activities indeed. Observing, role-playing and making choices. It's more of a real RPG, than todays action-packed hack and slash games with rpg elements, that claim to be ones.  I was blown away by the amount of lore and dialogue you encounter as soon as you enter the first city. Of course, you could probably skip and brush through most of it, but where's the fun in that?  The diversity of characters is huge: there's this robot who wants to have kids, a girl that carries around a rock with a god living in it, a ghostly woman that kills you, so she can talk to you inside your mind. Every one of them has a quest. Every one of them has a back story that is neatly interwowen with the lore and connected to other people. Everything comes together into a living, convincing world!  The locations in this game are simply beautiful. You can stumble across huge, ancient constructs spanning several screens, long-silent or repurposed to everyday needs. Next to it there would be hundreds-feet-high cliffs with crumbling houses built into them, statues, palaces or market stalls.  And almost every ancient artefact you can interact with, that is, if you can remember how...  Granted, there is very little combat, and when there is, you can wriggle your way out of it, most of the times. However this was true of the original Torment as well. Nevertheless, you have a decent amount options if you do decide to engage in skull splitting, even if only for fun or blood-thurstiness. ;) There are abilities, spells, and numerous magic artifacts, whose sole purpose is to be used during a fight for a variety of effects.  Bottom-line: If you love good writing, superb art, if you're into original, non-cliche techno-fantasy worlds - pick it up!

I backed this game on Kickstarter, so it's been a couple years coming. Unfortunately the finished product isn't anything more than an excellent argument for why crowdsourced games can be a bad idea.  This game doesn't stand on its own merits and, really, was never intended to. From the beginning it was pitched as a spiritual successor to Planescape: Torment, which was a well-written novel expressed through a bad (by today's standards) game engine. Much of the appeal of PS:T came from exploring the incredibly cool and weird D&D setting of Planescape where it all went down, and the equally cool and weird setting of Numenera is a good fit for an unofficial sequel. So that's all well and good. The other main part of PS:T's greatness was its cast of characters.  Tides does an uneven job of bringing the Numenera setting to the computer screen. There's a lot of awkward callbacks to Planescape that feel fairly out of place in the Ninth World, like the "Endless War" made up for Tides for no apparent reason other than because Planescape: Torment featured the Blood War, but that can probably get away with being called fanservice. The deliberate references and callbacks to Planescape: Torment make this game weaker, but they're obligatory since the only reason anyone funded this project was out of nostalgia.  The developers clearly lacked a strong understanding of how Numenera plays, or at least were shaky on how to best translate the feel of the tabletop into video game form. Cyphers, which are supposed to be the star of the setting, are reduced to a series of bland grenades and healing potions that are just sold by vendors on the street. Since the game actively punishes getting into fights, both because enemies tend to be stronger and more numerous than you and because the "Crisis" combat system is tedious and awful, the vast majority of items and abilities are useless garbage which you nevertheless must manage at least a little because they kept the Cypher Sickness mechanic.  It's difficult for me to find things worth writing about this game. Wherever there are game mechanics you're much better off avoiding them--fighting is boring at best, frustratingly unfair at worst. Approaching the game as a piece of interactive fiction, something has to be said about the Tides: they're a really bizarre morality concept which the game makes a big deal about but which are way too vague and unintuitive to actually become meaningful. Basically, depending on your words and actions your levels in the five Tides go up and down. There is text to indicate what the Tides are supposed to be about but there's a complete disconnect between your choices and the fluctuations of the Tides. If you're compassionate it's a toss-up between Gold and Indigo, if you're brash it's a toss-up between Red and Silver. Oftentimes they'll mix and on rare oddball occasions you'll lose out on Tides, even though most of the time even if you go completely against what a particular Tide is supposed to be about it doesn't drop. You're likely to gain a lot of Blue just because they hand out Blue for exhausting dialogue options and asking a lot of questions--which is standard operating procedure for these games so that you don't miss out on content. I have no idea what the point is. The Last Castoff is an aggressively blank brick of a character and most of your dialogue is gormlessly asking questions and whining that you have no idea what is going on. It's a pretty big letdown compared to the Nameless One from Planescape, or the main characters of the Dragon Age series, or the Exile from Knights of the Old Republic II. Even the utterly generic PCs of Icewind Dale II had more character, and they were solely defined by their class, alignment, and who was speaking to the NPCs at the time.  Since the main character is a blank slate, it falls to the NPC companions to carry the weight of the storytelling, which they don't. This is an area where the developers constantly inviting comparisons to Planescape: Torment hurts them hardest. The party members here aren't exactly on the level of Dak'kon or Fall-From-Grace or Morte. Most have no compelling connection or tie to the Last Castoff, which already is a problem, and they don't really do much to endear themselves to the player either. The developers chose to make them all very optional, which also means that they can't develop as a team, as was done in Dragon Age or KotOR. They feel like hirelings with short stories attached that they can spew out if you bother to ask them.  Look, if you really want Planescape: Torment, just (re)play that game. Tides is boring. Tides is awkward. It very painfully wants to be something that it very clearly lacks the creativity to be. There's lots of little design decisions that add up to big frustrations and immersion-breaking laughs at just how pretentious and absurd this game can be. For example: the lengthy sidequest where if you rest an arbitrary number of times the quest-giver literally falls off a cliff off-screen for no reason. Or how about the numerous (optional, to be fair(?)) fights where if you do choose to [Attack] your enemies all get to go first, with no possibility of you getting the drop on them (of course you can't position your party or do anything to prepare before the fight, I guess because someone decided that would make it too easy). I stumbled upon VA-11 Hall-A: Cyberpunk Bartender Action (Vallhalla) before it's release.  The artstyle and soundtrack both pretty SNES-esque IMO, got me hooked immediatley (actually it's inspired by PC-98 adventure games).  Try listening to it, while reading further:   https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpJCs-OJqfM  The fact that it's a Visual Novel kept me from buying it at first, but then I realized it's not like "those" other V Novels out there. And so it became one of my favourite games out there.   It has a great story, which is told almost completly by, you guessed it, bartending. Many different characters enter the bar, and depending on what you serve them, they'll  tell you their stories, and in result you also learn about Jills ( the protagonist) story.   The stories are mostly about the problems they face in their town "Glitch  City", news or their favourite Idol. The game is about the STORIES. Not stereotypes, nudity or boobs. In fact there's even a female character that tries to hide her breastsize, and you can learn why she does so. The humour is mature and great, and especially the "sexbot" is great at sexual innuendos.     Every day, before you start to work, you can check news, boards and blogs on Jills tablet. They are "lore"heavy, a reflection of our life, or just supid/funny. (There's a newspost about a new law that wearing socks in sandals is now illegal).  The soundtrack is a mix of many things. It sounds a lot like old game soundtracks, while still being futuristic. Other then that they have a wide range, most of them are pretty calm, which fits the game, other of them are fastpaced. Some song have an E-guitar ,a calm piano,  or heavy bass, but all have a lot of synth in them.  Everytime you start your day at the bar, or reenter after taking your break, you can switch the songs you want to hear in the musicbox. You can fill all slots with one song aswell, if you wish to do so.  I highly recommend  giving the game a try if you are interested, even if the genre of V. Novel doesn't appeal to you.  Get some snacks, a cold drink , get comfortable and  enjoy. VA-11 Hall-A has it's own charm, and the way it tells it story is just awesome.  In case you want to learn even more, check out the games website:   http://waifubartending.com/  Go ahead, it's time to mix drinks and change lives! :)

I really wanted to like this game, but I feel like it is complicated just for the sake of complexity, and it loses the fun because of it. To me, it felt like a project more than a game.  I love Don't Starve. It's difficult, and challenging, and has a lot to learn and explore, but the basics of the game are simple enough to jump in and play, and the progression makes sense. You see things on the ground to pick up, and you pick them up. You put a stick and rock together and it makes a tool. You put a bunch of flowers together and make a flower hat, and that makes you happy. If you're hungry, eat a berry or carrot or cook a rabbit. You can complete basic tasks easily and intuitively in Don't Starve, and that gives you the time and energy to experiment with more complex crafting and developing strategies for other elements of the game.  In Oxygen Not Included, everything is complicated and nothing is intuitive. The whole screen is filled with menus, and buttons, and drop downs. There is no tutorial. You don't know what's important and what isn't. You're bombarded with countless possible tasks, and you aren't sure which are necessary and which can wait, and doing them doesn't make sense.  Are you hungry? Make a generator, and a battery, and cables, and a food production machine, which needs dirt and water to make food. Huh? Or you can tell it to make food with other things, but who knows what those are, or how you find/make them, or if that kind of food is better somehow.   And every single thing you need to do is similarly a multi-step process that is intentionally complex, and doesn't make sense. Want Oxygen for your people, make an oxygen generator. But if your living area is too small, it will stop working. How does that make any sense?   It doesn't feel fun, it feels like a chore. Sometimes a menu or informational panel would pop up and I don't know if it was because something in the game triggered it, or I pushed a button or clicked something, but now I have more clutter fighting for my attention.   The user interface was poorly designed, the game was overly complex, there was no tutorial for even basic concepts, and the needs of your characters were nonsensical and illogical. I wish I could give this a 'Neutral' review, but I think I lean more to the negative side, so that's what I'm going with. This is not a *bad* game, but I haven't particularly enjoyed it. I definitely was hoping for a slightly casual, but skill-based coop game to blow off steam. The first few missions are really fun - hectic action, looks and runs well, fun combat and challenge. But quickly the problems became apparent.  The game's systems are incredibly opaque. Power? Illusion? Endless crafting and salvaging menus? Crates and quests? Nothing has any tutorial or explanation. HUD symbols have no explanation. The difficulty spikes can be frustrating as well, and lots of time can be wasted for no material gain if you die late in the level. This is more of an opinion gripe than anything else. There are a ton of different weapons, but most feel quite similar, and the enemies are extremely samey.  But my central gripe with the game is that it just isn't that fun. The core gameplay is quite repetitive, at least at lower character levels. Block, occasionally push or dodge, use one of two attacks. Occasionally, shoot your ult at a special/elite enemy. It feels like ammo is quite scarce unless you have a ammo retrieval skill, so I was reluctant to use my ammo. The game just feels very spammy and there aren't many interesting decisions to be made. Maybe things are different when queueing in a party at very high difficulties.  I can only speak to my experience which was admittedly casual from the start. I was not looking for a deep game, but I guess I wanted something with a little more flair. Nothing really feels veryunique, aside from the setting/enemies which can be unusual. I wouldn't pay more than $9.99 for this game.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance is, in my opinion, a great RPG game. However, there are some issues with it which I will list in this review.  The storyline so far has been involved and challenging. I haven't completed the main story yet but so far I am finding it engaging.  There are a multitude of side quests to complete which have a large range of activites, it's not all combat based which I enjoy greatly. One minute you will have to fight bandits, the next you will be sneaking into a house at night to steal a trinket of some sort and the next you will be taking your sweetheart on a date, there is a large range of activites to complete.   The combat is hard and there is a learning curve and it will take a while to get used to. I still, myself, haven't gotten used to it 100% but this adds tensions before any fights I get into which I actually find more immersive. You're not overpowered compared to enemies, you're all balanced so if you're not spot on, you will die or get seriously injured.  You cannot save anywhere on the map unless you consume a Saviour Schnapps which also counts as an alcoholic beverage so you will get merry on this. I didn't have issues with them like others have saying they're expensive because you get quite a lot for free at the start of the game and if you use them wisely, these will last until you either have more money or can create them at an alchemy bench.  It is wise to save often when possible so make use of sleeping in game, however, be aware that you cannot oversleep and the game will make you aware of this when you try.  The small details in this game make it for me. Cleaning yourself and your weapons in fear of judgement from other characters is a big plus and adds to the RPG experience. I also enjoy the reputation system and the diversity in dialog options.  Now onto the cons.  The game isn't well optimised at the moment in my opinion so it can look quite clunky and there are some clipping issues when it comes to armour and tack for your mount. However, I am allowing for the fact it is a new game and hopefully this will be fixed.  Bugs seem to affect everyone differently and, luckily, I haven't encountered any game breaking bugs (touch wood), just a few inconvenient ones that I have made clear in their forums.  All in all this is a very enjoyable, immersive RPG experience and also very educational. You can enjoy the game for what it is and learn the history of the Czech Republic back in the 1400's. Being a history nerd I enjoy that a lot.  9/10 Would definitely have another sesh with Father Godwin!

I'm conflicted on this. I adored Enemy Unknown/Within, and XCOM 2 improves upon those games in many respects. The customization is great, and (fixable) optimization issues aside, it looks amazing. Simply put, I play strategy games to (shock) strategize. If the occasional mission warrants I move fast (bomb diffusal), okay. I didn't mind it in EU/EW, but here it's every freakin' mission. You're constantly encouraged to avoid detection and set up ambushes, while simultaneously having Central yell at you that, unless you touch the magic objective RIGHT F***ING NOW, the world will end. You have one, maaaaybe two turns if you're lucky to set up, and then you gotta go H.A.M. to make it in time.  And it continues into the strategic overview as well. You're constantly bombarded with things to do, while being forced to plow through the campaign or be subjected to more aliens than Texas.  I can't understand how anyone thought this was going to be a good idea. Some say it was to curb Overwatch, but that could be done by tweaking overwatch range/accuracy/damage. There was no need to take a legitimate mechanic for bomb diffusal or hostage rescue, and impose it on the entire game.
The game, I have heard, is good. I wouldn't know though, since it's constantly crashes. Also, that mission timer...? I want to enjoy my game, not being rushed all the freaking time.

Be sure to try out the classic control scheme, allowing for animation cancels, if the regular one isn't to your liking. Traversal and puzzles are still a large part of the game and provide a nice change of pace from constant fighting. Character-wise, Fury is not as easily likable as her brothers, though she has a nice arc throughout the story and I came to respect her, as she learned and changed for the better. This game remind me of way back in the day, when video games first came out in arcades. We were bored out of our minds, so any meaningless game seemed fun to us...feeding quarters into the machines just to play the same old same old patterns with the only goal of beating our previous high score. That describes this game perfectly. If you have nothing to do, and all you want is a brainless exercise in repeating the same old patterns over and over again until you beat some sort of high score or something, you might enjoy this game. The art is cool (obviously inspired by Darkest Dungeon), music is decent, voice acting decent...but the goofy characters you run into every time you die, which is often, get old fast. I'd say this game is best suited to very casual players who have 30 minutes to an hour to burn through every day or two. Not really a game you can dive into and lose yourself in the cool story and world. Much more of a light pass-time with no particular goal other than grinding to grind.  OK. I'm further into the game and have beaten the first boss. For a while there, the game was growing on me as I mastered the very unwieldy controls and managed to kill that boss...finally. Guess what? You don't get to continue your game after that boss when you die. You go all the way to the very beginning and you need to play through all the rooms in that level and defeat that same level boss over and over ever single time you try a run. Now the grind is just getting absurd. Even after you beat a boss you have to beat it over and over every single time along with all the other bosses. Kudos to the die-hards who manage to finish this thing because they must have sunk some serious chunks of their actual lives into playing the exact same levels and encounters hundreds, if not thousands, of times.  Ugh. I've had it. I cannot grind another second on this grind fest of relentless grinding where you grind and grind and grind just to get the reward of grinding some more.  They make you get these diamonds eventually, and they make it seem like you'll get something really cool or useful when you get them. All they do is unlock the ability to see your game stats and that is it. What a gigantic letdown.

The gameplay is quite satisfying and snapy, but it gets really tedious in the later levels where enemies are very tanky and the visuals really get in the way of the action and make it hard to react to enemies. As far as the story goes, as I've said it starts really good but because of the rouge-like nature it really started to annoy me because some questlines basically started when the game decided to spawn the correct characters to start the quests, and the true final payoff of the story was kind of  lackluster in my opinion. Now don't get it twisted 50 hrs and 100% achievements don't stand for nothing. If you really enjoy rogue-likes you could do far far worse than hades, but that is all this game is: a very pretty looking rogue-like with and interesting setting, somewhat engaging story and cluttered combat. Out of the 50 hours I played I enjoyed maybe somewhere around 30 of them

I finally got around to finishing NieR Automata and.. it isn't as much as a masterpiece as people made it out to be when it first released, at least in my opinion. A lot of areas of the open-world map are quite lazily done and those parts of the map have areas that are quite repetitive (like the desert for example) and not to mention the game also runs like absolute ass. So you maybe thinking that If I'm talking so negatively about this game then why recommend it at all? Well, the truth is that this game is worth playing for just for the story and the soundtrack alone which are both amazing. The story isn't anything perfect but it's incredibly unique and very  philosophical, the level of detail that has clearly been put into the story is amazing as well. the only parts of the game that make it worth playing is the story and the soundtrack, I stand by this because the issue with the game is that the design philosophy of the combat in several areas and the world itself feels like something more akin to an late PS2 or a early PS3 title, and that kind of design philosophy hasn't aged well and could definitely be improved so much more, in the modern day especially when considering that the game limitations aren't as low as they used to be. With all that said the game had quite a low budget so I can't hit it on too much for those aspects, I honestly think that this game could have been improved so much if it had a higher budget. Hopefully due to the overwhelming success of this game a future title could improve those aspects of the game, I am very excited to seeing where the story goes after this game as well.

At time of review I've played for 69 hours (nice) and I can firmly say that this game has some pretty cool **** going on.   Pros -If you have the DLCs there are a ton of clans to pick from, each with different strategies, perks, relics, and even clan specific techs. Even without the DLCs there are a solid number of clans to pick from. -The game is actually just really nice to look at -Map Generation tends to be pretty diverse with its choice of tiles, and the game actively tends to avoid giving you a **** spawn point -Certain unique tiles can spawn and every single one of them is worth going for, ranging from making every unit in your military stronger, to stealing the unique techs of other clans, to spawning in really pissed off ghosts that practically ignore projectiles and make the enemy clans go cry on the forums and refuse to breed -The music, oh man the music of this game is so good  Cons -The AI can sometimes be, well, REALLY stupid. They will frequently watch your warchiefs/unique clan leaders walk out of their territory with 5 HP and just let them go instead of chasing for the kill which would set you back massively on resources -Large clusters of units can make it borderline impossible to manually select an enemy to focus down since character models can overlap, but generally in those massive fights it's just a slugfest anyway, so it's not too terrible -Some clans are a struggle at first to figure out how you're supposed to play them, due to either niche strategies, or unclear text. A great example is the clan of the bear, where you get a giant armored bear (shocker) that states it cannot go into enemy territory. One might think this means it can only be in your own territory, but it can run in unclaimed territory as much as it wants, meaning that you can expand at ridiculous rates early on since the bear can fight just about any neutral group of units you are likely to encounter near your spawn point. -No baseline HP regen for clan units. This one is mostly a personal gripe. Neutral units while out of combat will slowly regenerate over time, however any units belonging to a clan MUST be in ally territory and you MUST have healers assigned for them to be healed barring specific tech options for specific clans IE Bear clan units heal automatically while in friendly territory in the winter. This can make the early game a real slog as healers can be a major part of your food production, and stop gathering food when healing  If you enjoy real time strategy games, while this one might not be the most crazy in depth, it is a ton of fun to play, quick to get into, and quick to figure out barring a few clans. I will wholeheartedly recommend this game to anybody just looking for a fun time that even slightly enjoys RTS.

This game is just pointless.   I've been trying so hard to like it, but it's ultimately frustrating to do so. Prepare to die because of: - Boredom: where's the story? Random stereotyped characters thrown into the carnage. - The game mechanics: 3 stances, several types of weapon and you'll be using always the same 2. Guaranteed. - The avalanche of useless items enemies will drop: stopped reading the item descriptions at minute 15 - The inventory management: Jesus Christ, Too Human did a better job than this - The absence of any kind of balance in the fights: the same skeleton that will tear you apart at level 1, will still kick your ass at level 120.  - The boss fights: depending on your build, they're either stupidly frustrating or baffling easy.  - The abuse of the same assetts: you've fought this boss? why not fighting again 3 more times. The combat system is great, the graphics/music/sound are good, everything else kind of sucks.  - The same few enemies are recycled throughout the whole game. This is really the most dissapointing thing. It doesn't matter how good the combat is if you are fighting the same 5 enemies over and over again. - Boss fights basically consist of keeping your distance and quickly running in when you see an opening, hitting the boss, and running away. It doesn't feel like you are really engaging the boss like it does in say, Dark Souls. - The loot system is just atrocious. You pick up dozens and dozens of items with an endless number of obscure stats, with no way to tell if one piece of loot is actually better than another. Flushing all the garbage out of your inventory gets old really quickly. - Levels are overly maze-like and level design in general isn't anything to write home about. - Levels are recycled for boring and tedious side missions. The game would have been better if they just took these out altogether. - Bizarre and inscrutable plot and dialogue-laden cut scenes. After the first several cutscenes I just started skipping them automatically because I couldn't care less about what these people were talking about. The main bad guy just looks silly. - A comparatively minor point, but this game has one of the most unintuitive skill/upgrade user interfaces I've ever seen

I was really looking forward to going through the story... until I realized there wasn't really a story.  You play as Mae, an obnoxious selfish young woman who somehow manages to make the worst possible choice at every given opportunity. I thought this would be a story about maturing, coming to terms with life, etc (which is a theme that crops up now and again in fairness). Instead its 10 hours of small talk, pointless activities and just... nothing. At the part where things actually get interesting and you think something will finally happen... it just ends.  I genuinely like some of the characters, and was excited to see what kind of arc they would have. However, no matter what happened in the 'story', what traumatic experience or arguments would occur, just like a sitcom everything would go back to normal almost immediately.  This could have been an excellent game. I don't know what happened but it all just feels so... unfinished and unsatisfying, but perhaps that's the point?

After roughly 30 hours of game play...I'm bored. To be honest, I was bored after about 12 hours.   https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997797838  I bought this hoping it would scratch the Stardew Valley itch well enough, although I am fully aware that it is entirely its own thing. But there is one really big problem:  Everything boils down to repeatedly pressing a button, and then waiting for something to finish crafting. Rinse repeat.   https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997797935  That aside...  Game focuses on building, crafting, and improving the town versus a lot of emphasis on farming (although they do have that + ranching). Very kid friendly, and combat is very, very simple and not challenging.   Pros: -Wide variety of progression options. -Tons of crafting. -World graphics & design are nice. -Lots of mining and adventuring. -Simple game that feels rewarding. -NPC voices are mostly great. -Furniture and home decor add buffs/stats to your character. Which is really cool!  Cons: -Main character's voice is one of the worst I've heard in any video game. After speaking with friends who've played this game, 2 of the 3 stated they muted in game voices because they were so irritating.  -Caves/Abandoned Ruins are visually boring and dull. It's a big room full of dirt you can mine into. You can scan for items, but it all looks like an after thought. It becomes very monotonous and boring -Character feels far to young to have relationships or marriage with adults.  -Lots of grinding -Lots of fetch quests. -Haven't unlocked everything, but world/map feels...quite small. -Lacks replay value -Lacks depth  It kind of does trick but could be a lot better. Glad I got this in a Humble Bundle deal. Would not pay full price. Possibly worth playing if you are a fan of Stardew Valley or other Harvest Moon-esque games. Just understand it is very simple and lacks much of any challenge. Ideal for kids.   6/10 - Polished and enjoyable enough to squeeze 30 hours out of it, but boring and simple to the point where I can't give it higher of a score. Won't be recommending *except to friends with kids.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997798220

Do you like levels purposely designed to frustrate you?  What about dying over and over until you time a jump absolutely perfectly, only to proceed to the next area just to do the same thing again? An extremely basic story with no real depth? The occasional hipster quips thrown at you by characters that can admittedly be funny/cute at times? Then you may enjoy Celeste. For the players skilled at platformers with a great deal of patience, this may be an amazing game.  For the average players, not so much.  Now, I'm not saying it's a bad game by any means but it's overall design seems intended to be frustrating rather than fun.  Success is heavily dependent on perfect execution of jumps.  You will die playing this more than Dark Souls.  I know I did.    There is an assisted mode which makes the game infinitely easier, however, playing on that mode defeats the purpose or satisfaction of completing the game IMO.  That is not to say the game should not have an assisted mode, because it definitely needs one for those who would like to bypass the challenge.  I played without enabling assist mode once and it sure was more frustrating than fun.  Perhaps I would have had more fun playing with a handicap, yet it just wouldn't have been equally satisfying.  So, for someone who has an average skill level with platformers, and refuses to play with any sort of handicap, I absolutely do not recommend this.  The frustrating level design coupled with sloppy game pad controls makes for a subpar experience.  The controls by themselves are pretty good but the level design and some of its mechanics make the controls not so great (on a 360 controller). Go play Ori and the Blind Forest if you haven't already.  Much better across the board.

The game will only become powerful by the end if you grow a love and attachment for the world you play in, and it never really gives us that. No re-occuring characters, no backgroud or reason for it's exsistance at all, it just throws you in this strange, unexplained place for a few hours and expects you to value it by the end. It's a shame, with more thought towards the player having a bond with the world it could've been an amazing emotional rollorcoaster. Sadly it was hardly that.  That, plus long, repetitive exploring through the same disorienting map gets old fast. Game makes you feel stupid frequently, and expects you to understand things you don't. Even the essential buildings and items are easy to miss, and account for hours of dull and frustrating time trying to find the minimal amount of things you need. Some puzzles are badly explained and are almost impossible without using a walkthrough multiple times. Also, having a mac makes it worse when some PC puzzles don't even work (the 'easily acessible place'), and again would've been impossible without using walkthroughs.  I really, really want to give this a good review, but the amount of pitfalls it has is just too much to make it really enjoyable.  (hours played may not be accurate, I do a lot of gaming offline)
