Original review, after about 1.5 hours: Obviously I haven't played this game very much, so I'll update this review if my mind changes (which it very well could). But so far, I'm unimpressed. The game is chock-full of boring gameplay, ugly environments, average story, and ridiculous 4th-wall breaks. The "puzzles" are also annoying and time consuming, and require more trial and error than real puzzle solving skills. So far, I have yet to find the charm or hidden beauty most everyone seems to find in this game, but I'm going to try to finish the game to see if there's more than meets the eye.  Edit after beating the game: This game is hands down the worst game I have ever played. Everything I said before this edit still holds true, but I am feeling even more strongly about the negatives after I have beaten the game.  First off, the puzzles and gameplay are horrendous. Nothing has any logic attached to it, and I found myself reaching for a walkthrough constantly because the puzzles don't require skill, they require trying a bunch of random stuff until something works, which usually means walking around the map for an hour looking for items. I am just not invested in puzzles that don't require puzzle solving skills. The two puzzles (the goat and color code puzzles) that required some actual thought and gameplay felt like a breath of fresh air. A game should have gameplay? Right?  Next, the environments and art are as ugly as could be. Obviously the still illustrations look great, but THAT ISN'T THE GAME. The game should look nice while you're playing it. Every environment has washed out colors, disgusting pixel art character models, and the same buildings over. and over. and over again. It makes any atmosphere this game could've had go down the drain.  Finally, the story is mediocre at best. I didn't find the ending as emotional as everyone said it should be, partially because I wasn't invested in any of the characters or the world they inhabit from the get-go. (I will also say that I didn't go into the final section completely blind, but I don't feel like that made much of a difference.) No matter what ending you choose, you don't get to see the consequences, which makes the entire game feel meaningless. Your actions should have effects on the game world for them to feel like it matters.  I feel like I shouldn't be saying that this is the worst game I've ever played, but here's my thinking. This game is absolutely unfun and boring, but it isn't bad enough to cross into the "so bad it's good" territory. There is absolutely nothing I can pull from this, and it just felt like a complete waste of time. I'm also not usually such a big contrarian, so don't tell me I'm only saying this to be different from everyone else. I absoutely hate this game.  (also it would be nice if they deleted the malware. you can't even close the game from task manager in some of the parts? huh?)  Edit 2: I forgot to mention how much the soundtrack sucks. Playing the same three notes over and over again with some weak drums isn't good music. Come on guys. It makes me want to fall asleep even more than the game does by itself.

I keep trying to love this game, but under its quality designs, there really is nothing worth playing. Like many roguelikes, you end up stuck in an endless cycle of losing and starting over. Worse so, the game requires you to up difficulty to progress, and you do only to experience suffering all over. Very few of the enemies are fairly designed, and a couple seconds is all it takes to kill a single run that was going perfectly until then.  Before I begin, know that everything I list is true, but only after a certain amount of play in the game will you see it for yourself. To put it bluntly, the multiple playthroughs and grind required to get to the true end of the game are immense, and in this time difficulty will go from difficult but survivable into insane RNG bullcrap that no person should be forced to endure. Many people use mods to increase the grinding rate and skip the bullcrap, but this game sucks by default.  Here are some examples of awful terrible designs in this game: 1: The random mechanics obviously. Since your level ups and loadout will be random based on what you can find, you can be screwed that way. Most weapons are not all that useful, and some are terribly lacking in use. Sometimes you will not find a single legendary item, sometimes you will find 2 or more. There are just so many ways the RNG hurts you, but the best way to explain how RNG is awful is by comparing it to the minor issues in other games. Remember that time in another game where the hitbox was not so great and you died? Well, imagine that 100 times over because RNG has a habit of making every minor issue much much worse because you cannot even take grasp of a single good thing in this game before the game decides that RNG should also take it away. Enemy placement too is awful as a result, but that brings me to #2. 2: Awful enemies. The problem is not that they are difficult. Let me give you a few examples from the first level. So, there is an enemy type that shoots its projectile at you. Normally, this would not be a problem, but the enemy can see you through walls, and the bullet can pierce walls. It is not fun in the least. As you up the difficulty, which you will do later on, it only gets worse. A new enemy shows up in the very first level that can rapidfire attack you with slashes and kill you in a single combo. Both of these enemies have random placement, and both show up in the first level. The varied enemy type would normally not be awful, but the lack of balancing and terribly random placement, which sometimes results in dodging two of those piercing projectiles, one claw comboman, a flying man with his swords, and a shield guy wandering nearby that prevents you from properly countering and you have nothing but a mess. It gets worse and worse, you have been warned. 3: Unlockables..... So you got further, got a blueprint, grinded a bunch, and now you are finally able to randomly come across that item in the map, which you will lose upon death because this game hates you. Abilities are unlocked the same way.  This game spreads content thin and is painful to play. It looks pretty, but is a pile of garbage and cheap awful design ideas.

Here's the thing, if you're really fiending for some sort of metriodvania styled game and you've already played Axiom Verge and Hollow Knight, then maybe its ok for you to drop some money on this game itch that scratch for a weekend.  Even then, I find it a bit odd that this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews. I found it to be incredibly average.  What I think this game has going for it is that it does have some pretty impressive pixel artistry and some very good animation, and I don't think the game is really all that "bad", its a complete game which is something I can't say for a lot of games now days. Hell, I'm even fine that its a short game, it can take about 4 hours to beat. The problem is that it kind of lacks personality for a game that is supposed to be story driven, all I know about the game is that your trying to kill a queen because a curse spread to your land and thats litterately it. The combat was incredibly bland, all you have are arrow shots, a roll, and the same 3 hit combo to get you throughout the entire game. What makes it challenging is the artifical difficult of being hit about 3 times is enough to kill you and reset your progress.  Knowing where to travel next was a pain because, unlike other metriodvania's, this game doesn't really give you new power ups that warrant a reason for you to explore previous areas. You just get a key and have to try to remember which door you might have passed earlier that its supposed to fit to. The soundtrack of the game was ok, there was a song I liked in there somewhere but too much of it felt like generic japanese fantasy music.  I think my biggest gripe is that you can tell this game wants to be Dark Souls but fails to come close capturing the essence of the series. When you use your bellflower its the exact same animation as crushing a soul gem. There's a fight where the boss lights her sword with the exact same animation as using Charcoal Pine Resin in dark souls. The background of Karst Castle looked like I was back in Kanehurst from Bloodborne.Now, there's not problem borrowing ideas from other games, it shows your influences and there's a reason why so many games nowadays are borrowing mechanics and the overall vibe of the dark souls games. The problem is that I didn't see anything in Momodora that made me feel like I was playing a game influenced by Dark Souls but rather a game trying to be Dark Souls with a chibi aesthetic.   Look, the guy who made this game is a talented indivdual. I can't make a video game, I've tried, I don't have the patience and I'm not as good of an artist as he is. I want to see what else he puts out in the future, but here's advice as to what can be improved upon.  As far as Metriodvanias are concerned, the games are usually about the journey of the hero and watching as they, and the player, grow more powerful throughout their journey. Provide some upgrades that improve the way the character moves throughout the world. Some of the basic stuff seen in other games is additional jumps, wall jumping, sprinting, climbing, etc. Also, use these upgrades as reasons to include environmental puzzles for the players to return to and solve. Use these upgrades are reasons for a player to be able to progress to a new area they otherwise wouldn't have been able to access yet.  As for what makes Dark Souls special, its not just the combat, its the world. Leave a trail of breadcrumbs for the in areas that maybe have some sort of significance to the story. Tell a story to the player without using words. Especially with how great of an artist this guy is, I feel like that would be his strong suit here.   So yeah, overall, I played the game through to completion and I appreciate that it was a short game, but I think there's a lot of progress that can be made on future games. The main reason why I'm marking this as a game I don't recommend is because there's already games out there that do the same thing but do it better, and while I'm the type of person to spend a ton of money on steam, if a friend has 10 bucks and asks me which game to buy between Hollow Knight and Momodora I'm going to say Hollow Knight.

Enter the Gungeon is a game I do enjoy quite a bit.  However, I'm so deeply conflicted as to some very basic design principles the game uses, that I can't really recommend it in good conscience despite some of its good points.  On the surface, this is a gorgeous game with great sound design.  And I think a lot of people will be won over by that enough to get something out of the game.  And that's fine.  But this is by far, by leaps and bounds, the most RNG-dependent roguelite I have ever encountered.  When things are going well, when the game sees fit to give you guns that feel good to use, the gameplay on offer here is a treat.  You get to participate in these cinematic-feeling gun battles, flipping around, kicking over tables and sending explosive barrels rolling into crowds of enemies, hammering away with your guns.  It's good stuff.  And the boss battles can be truly intense, stand-out examples of great bullet hell design.  On the flipside, when the game doesn't give you good guns, it becomes a far worse and more tedious slog than even the worst runs in Isaac.  The main problem here is that enemies are bullet spongy, and bosses particularly so.  Coupled with a vast selection of guns (of which, less than half are fun to use, and most of the good ones are locked away behind a shop unlock system), and you have a recipe for a massive slog, particularly in the early game when you don't have much unlocked.  Just trying to consistently get past the first floor to unlock the gun shop was a tedious nightmare of dead-end runs.  I've played the game long enough now to see some good runs.  I've pulled the lever on the slot machine enough times to see that there's good stuff on offer here, from time to time between hopeless runs spent plinking away at enemies with little to no indication you're doing anything to them.  Every so often you'll get a big laser beam or a prototype railgun or a crystalline machine gun or something.  Those are great runs, because the way those guns feel to fire makes up for the fact that enemies don't really react to being shot in a satisfying way, and some of the good guns have high enough damage to make up for the crazy amounts of HP everything has.  When it's clicking, this is a really great game.  The problem is, when it's not clicking, there is nothing you can do but die and pull the lever again.  There is a lot to love here.  But I question whether it's worth the price of admission, and whether it's worth the tedium of dealing with it when it's not going your way.  There are a host of roguelites on the market these days, and most if not all of them deal with RNG in better ways than Gungeon does.  EtG has no real mitigating factors for dealing with bad runs, nothing that can help to smooth the curve.  And for that, despite its stellar highs when the RNG is being nice, I have to say I can only recommend it provisionally, to those who are willing to put up with some truly boring, frustrating between-times.  The fixes are simple: keys need to be cheaper to buy in the store, or chests need to not be locked.  The list of guns should be pruned to reduce the number of bad ones in the item pool.  And the game desperately needs some kind of RNG mitigator on par with Starward Rogue's shop inventory reroll, or Isaac's D6.  Without these things, though, it's a slog.

There's no dash, so you WILL watch yourself die, over and over, and then get that nice nostalgic 5 second long death screen where you watch all the money you've earned taken from you, followed by another 3 seconds to re-pick the same level on the map. Maybe that emulates the "good old days" but I personally find that frustrating when I'm already annoyed enough and just want a straightforward, no delay way to give it another go. There are a lot of good things to be said about Shovel Knight.  It is an inventive and well-crafted platformer that combines modern design elements with retro 8-bit graphics.  I would recommend this to anyone who likes very challenging platformers and liked old games like Mario Bros.  However, I would not recommend this game to people like me.  Although I've played some good platformers such as Rayman Legends, I didn't have a console when I was growing up and have no nostalgia for old games.  However, I picked up Shovel Knight after reading many reviews which called it the best game of 2014.  From my perspective, the game was usually just frustrating.  The final screen told me I died 330 times in the course of finishing this game.  I believe the vast majority of those were insta-kills, from falling.  The timing required is very precise---in many situations if you press the button a split second too early or too late you will be killed instantly.  Furthermore, if you take any damage from an enemy, they will often push you back, leading to another fall..  When this happens, no matter how much health you have, you die and will lose gold and be set back several screens.  No matter how much gold I started with, I rarely had any gold by the time I first got to a boss.  This made most of the game just depressing, as I felt the more I played the less gold I had.  Without gold, I couldn't buy many upgrades, which in turn made the next level even harder.  About my skill level, I guess I'm below average, but I don't think I'm that bad.  I loved Dark Souls for instance, but I feel Shovel Knight is even harder because there are fewer strategies and routes available, gold is easier to lose permanently, and most deaths come from insta-kills.  Also Dark Souls I felt was more atmospheric and included more RPG elements.  It's one thing to die in Dark Souls 15 times in a row in a tense battle with a huge Dragon.  It's another to die in Shovel Knight 15 times in a row just because you didn't manage to jump from one moving platform to another.  I think someone good at platforming would enjoy this game, but I think it's too hard to recommend to the average person.  If the developers added an easier difficulty setting I would recommend it whole-heartedly.

Shot a fallow deer 5 times, tracked it for over 1 real time hour, game crashed before I found it. 10/10 too much water  EDIT: TL;DR - Enjoyable, feels like a beta but very pretty with an iffy interface, less of a hunting game and more an animal shooting game. Bows are OP. No microtransactions.  After putting more time into this, I feel I can write a proper and serious review. At the time of writing, this game functions like beta. That said, despite being riddled with bugs and occasional crashes (though your mileage may vary on bugginess) this game is a graphically superb and worthy sibling to theHunter Classic, and I don't regret my purchase. My only major complaint is that they somehow managed to be less realistic in this game than Classic with both the general feel of the game and with animal behaviors - I feel I can describe it best in the way that Diablo 3 is not a dungeon crawler like D2, but a very large loot run. Similarly, you are placed in the vast reserve (and I do mean vast, the maps are colossal) with free reign over a never-ending hunt. It doesn't feel like hunting to me, it feels like animal shooting. Veterans of theHunter Classic (or even other hunting games, I suppose) might understand better than someone fresh to the genre.   Animals, particularly female deer, are still dumb as walking rocks with the added bonus of sometimes running you over on accident in their zeal to be the first to stand as close to you as possible. Bright side? They don't seem to magnetize toward you anymore - they go where the call was and stick around the immediate area. You're free to sprint like a madman with (seemingly) little consequence. In fact, it seems rewarding by the warning calls provided by animals, alerting you to their rough location. Just crouch and spam your callers. Move toward them for increased efficiency. Animals also seem to be very nonchalant about gunfire, even within ranges where they would probably reasonably hear it. They also seem to not mind returning to the same area where you butchered several herd members already. That said - the hunting pressure system seems to mostly work. Animals outside the group (if there was one) you killed from are very unlikely to enter the area when attracted to calls or scents. They do, on occasion, wander through to get somewhere else, though.  So far, weapons handle reasonably well and have satisfying sounds and animations, though I personally find the kick-up of recoil to sometimes be laughably extreme as an avid hunter in real life. The .243 is not as woefully pathetic as in Classic, and will absolutely do the work you need it to (until you can get the .270. Get it.). However, I recommend polymer tip bullets when available. They are a pleasant step up from the standard soft points, but certainly not a critical upgrade. Bows, however, seem grossly overpowered at the moment. Flesh wounds will have deer bleeding out in times comparable to decent rifle shots.  The interface is a bit cumbersome and lacks information (e.g. current weapon scores outside of the shop, experience until next level, return to main menu button) that I would like to have access to, although this is more of a personal gripe than a point against the game. Most of the nitpicky issues I have with menus and interface are personal beyond being unrefined. The map also has the tendency to find itself focused on anywhere except where you are when opened.  If I sound harsh on this game, it's not because these are glaring faults that should dissuade you from buying. This is a good game for the state it's in, but realize that it does have issues. I can recommend this to veterans of Classic that want a more streamlined and immediate hunting experience without fussing through menus and launchers or simply want to support Avalanche and Expansive Worlds. It's more of theHunter, what can I say? If you're on the fence or new to this series, perhaps stick with Classic until this game is fleshed out more.

To be frank, I can't for the life of me comprehend why this game has so many positive reviews. I mean, maybe I'm not that qualified to give my opinion on this, because I was already not really a big fan of the first game; but even though the first one had quite a few flaws, like the ridiculous story and a few irritating characters, overall it was still enjoyable to me. The sequel on the other hand takes all these flaws and turns them up to eleven:  - The story and murder cases this time around are utterly retarded and nonsensical.  - While the first game had a desperate and isolated atmosphere, truly fitting for the overall theme of despair, everything in this game just feels so goofy, exaggerated and overblown, that I couldn't take half of it seriously. Oh, and expect lots and lots of 4th wall breaks and self referential humor. Gotta love those, right?  - Somehow they managed to make the minigames even more annoying and unintuitive.  - The various characters, arguably the heart of these games, are so much worse than its predecessor, that it's not even funny. They are way too over the top, to the point that they just become grating to deal with. It goes way beyond being one dimensional or stereotypical; you just can't imagine these lunatics ever existing or functioning in real life. Everyone is crazy, everyone has a messed up past and strange values. One person is a glutton, she will think about nothing but food even in life and death situations. One character is sad someone turned out to be a murderer, the next moment she happily forgives him and recites the catchphrase of this game: "We gotta do our best, for his sake!" It all just feels so artificial.  It's a flaw a lot of japanese media has IMO: style over substance. Even if you bother to spend time with them, some character may reveal a superficial character flaw after a while, wich will never be brought up again and doesn't really matter. Oh, but you get their underwear as a reward. Aren't you glad you wasted time on this?  - The characters motivations for doing stuff and especially their motives for commiting murder dont make any lick of sense half of the time, which doesn't really help with endearing them to the player. It's probably not a good sign, that, while I was often saddened by the death of characters in the first game, I couldn't care less when someone died in this game. On the contrary, most of the time I was glad when someone finally bites the dust. It's fair to say I was pretty much on Monokuma's side the whole time.  -As for positive things: music is still enjoyable, graphics are alright and I encountered no bugs or glitches while playing.  Damn, that turned out longer than I wanted. So in conclusion, if you are like me and already had to massively strain your suspension of disbelief and tolerance for anime tropes during the first game, especially in regards to characters and story, avoid this one. Seriously, it feels like a different dev-team worked on this game. If you don't give a crap about this, get it on a sale, because that price is ridiculous for a VN.

First of all, I will open this by saying that I would recommend this game if it is on sale. I think the fact that many people have enjoyed it cannot be ignored, and you are perfectly entitled to enjoy and think positively of it. So why give it a negative review? I did enjoy this game and was glad I played it, but ultimately I could not feel positively about it for a number of reasons.  Overall, the style of gameplay is fun. If you can stomach the ultraviolence, it's really quite satisfying in a bloodthirsty sort of way. It's especially relieving to bludgeon that guard who's killed you 20 times to death with his own weapon. It forces you to think about how you are going to attack. The fact you can only take one hit offers a challenging mechanism where failure is not tolerated for a split second.  The look and feel is fits the era very well. I greatly enjoy top-down games like this one and I think in terms of gameplay it was a wise decision. The attention to detail however is questionable; it's fairly difficult to tell what many things actually are, and sometimes the art style can get in the way of gameplay (lose a knife amongst a pile of bodies and it's sometimes difficult to find it again). The spinning maps, whilst fitting in with the design, are sometimes very unpleasant and gave me motion sickness a few times - there is no option to turn them off. But this is just a small inconvenience. More annoying is how it's impossible to tell whether an object can be shot over or not (a fountain is inpenetratable, but a pile of boxes isn't).  The music is overall quite good. I was surprised by how hyped it is though. It sets the mood well but, after the same track has looped for the 100th time, it begins to do your head in. In the final levels the music is also distorted for what I presume is artistic effect but this fails; it simply turns out irritating. I found myself muting the music a lot. When I did this I could focus much better.  The difficulty curve is generally good at the start. As many point out, it's skilfully created so that you don't realise how far you are progressing until you go back and try an earlier level. This is something many games have tried and failed to implement. There are no hoops to jump through, no instructions left at various stages: only a few elements that get gradually introduced (such as dogs and guns). However, about half way through, this falls apart. The personal advancement you can get from the game levels out, and whilst some levels increase in difficulty as one would expect, others - completely out of place - are bizarrely quite easy. It leads to a very disjointed experience where you might spend half an hour or more on one level and five minutes on the next.  One of my troubles with the game is it cannot make up its mind as to what it wants to be. Is it a simple arcade fighting game? But the combat is too basic to really live up to the title, and the repetition is just too much. Is it a stealth game? I don't think the creators ever intended for it to be one, but if they did, they failed miserably - the AI is simply too crude.  Is it a puzzle game? Then it is irritatingly inconsistent. A puzzle relies on everything being near enough the same when you try it again - when the AI's behaviour seems to rely on a coin flip this does not measure up.  As far as I could decipher, enemies have three states: patrol, alert and attack. You have to be aware of how the AI works to beat a level. The problem here is that the AI is actually quite inconsistent. Often levels will require you to "bait" an enemy to get him to follow you to somewhere that's easy to dispose of him. In theory there is nothing wrong with this, but in practice it's pretty much anyone's guess whether the AI is going to take a few seconds to see you or do a split-second 180-degree spin and instakill you. The game relies on the mechanic that a gun will alert an enemy, but it's completely random as to who will be alerted. Sometimes, it's enemy across the map. Other times, the enemy in the room next door will completely ignore it. When you actually want the AI to come to you and be alerted, this is frustrating. The randomisation is cheap, and means that I rarely found any gratification in victory - only the feeling that the it had gone my way for once.  I found a number of bugs that frustrated me and only compounded my issues. Firstly, the game crashes a lot, at least on my computer. I got an average of about one crash every hour or so. Most of these crashes were to do with doors somehow, and it's no surprise, since doors themselves are a mess. It's easy to exploit the AI by standing in the door and letting it glitch out and swing to and fro; this will slow them down for some reason and make it easier to take them on. Sometimes a door will travel right through an enemy instead of knocking him down, especially if there are multiple ones around. Combat bugs are relatively common; I enjoyed performing a "hug of death" where you stand right in front of an armed enemy. For whatever reason, they will fire but cannot hit you, so you simply wait for them to deplete their ammo. It's an amusing but basic issue that should have been fixed. Dogs will often ending up circling around underneath you for some reason (making them impossible to attack) until they decide to kill you. The way bullets interact with walls is strange and often to kill an enemy coming around a corner you have to make sure your gun is pointed at a wide angle rather than perpendicular, otherwise your bullets will not hit. Hitboxes are sketchy too...  I did finish the game, if only to be able to sufficiently review it, and there were many times when I really had to force myself to continue. There comes a point where you will have attempted a level many, many times and failed. It's 2am, the music is going around and around, you're slumped in your chair and you think to yourself... "why am I actually playing this? What is my motivation to continue?"   The bonuses at the end of the level are something. If you get a high enough score you might get a weapon and/or a mask. Both of these have limited use. The masks are a clever mechanic that add perks - changing how you play. They're fairly interesting but I think the masks were too specific to ever make a massive difference. The weapons are virtually useless; you hardly ever actually get them. Regardless, it's very dispriting to spend an hour finishing a level only to get a glass bottle as a reward.  The second motivator is the story line. The story is... limited. In many games I have been motivated to continue an especially difficult level by wanting to continue the story line. In Hotline Miami, I can't say that any motivation existed. Though the ending is mildly interesting, it's really not fitting for how much time is spent on it, and a fairly big insult.  The only motivator I can think of after that is personal challenge and the score. These are fine, and will be different for everyone, but it's a sign of a half-baked game if these are the only [i]only[/i] motivating factor.  Ultimately, my biggest problem with Hotline Miami was boredom. The level design is sameish. The enemies are all the same. The difference between weapons is minimal. The fact you have to play the same level over and over again gets old, quickly. The story line is, up until the end, mostly unengaging. The boss fights are anticlimactic.  You can say that the repetition and difficulty is all part of the fun. You can apply the same principle to nailing jelly to the ceiling. It's a difficult task where you fail a lot of the times, come frustratingly close often, and maybe at one point succeed. That does not mean you feel good about the thankless task of having nailed jelly to the ceiling. You simply feel that you have wasted your time.

If you're looking for a game like those, then I urge you not to purchase this game for several reasons.  It is short. Painfully short. This is not a game you can sit down and enjoy an experience for a few nights. My brother and I beat this in a whopping 5 hours. 5 hours. Going as slow and steady as possible so as not to miss anything, it took 5 hours to explore every little nook and cranny and hidden "secrets". Half an hour of that time was dying, and maybe 45 minutes was dedicated to trying to learn about the world and looking around. So all in all, maybe 3 hours is all you'll really get out of this.  And then there's the exploring. Looking for secrets and clues and answers to the world you're thrown in is fun when the game doesnt explicitly tell you the plot. This game, however, does not tell you anything. And when you do go looking for your own answers, you are rewarded with nothing. There is no point to wasting any time looking for hidden things here. Its insulting. Rather than lore in what presents itself as an interesting world, you get collectables that pretty much amount to nothing.  Nothing is a key theme here. The game really offers you nothing. The game is much to short and frankly abrupt to really enjoy the atmosphere. The art is honestly great, but you're given very little to look at. The soundtrack is fitting for the enviornment, but you only ever really notice it at maybe 2-3 points in the game, and it has no weight to it when things really do start happening.  All in all, the game is short, does not reward you for taking your time to enjoy it, not at all immersive, and insulting on how you learn nothing and have to make up the answers to the plot yourself. You will most likely leave this game unsatisifed and feeling cheated out of what could have been a fun, mysterious horror setting journey. I do not recommend this.

Note: This review was written on Day 2 of Early Access. This game may change a great deal from this point forward. In short, it's an Early Access game that has Early Access problems. If you want to play a promising MMO "Beta", try it out. Read on for more thoughts. First, a word on the current storm of negative feedback surrounding Bless. This game was previously released in other countries. However, the North American version of Bless is Early Access. In other words, this game is NOT a finished product. The development team has stated, in so many words, that they are using the resources provided by Early Access to rebuild Bless into a new and better game. That said, In it's current state, the game is very playable. It's got a lot of great ideas, some original, and many reminiscent of other games. Though, there are a few bugs that range from the slightly annoying, to the downright irritating. The combat is where Bless shines. It's very smooth, and well animated. There's very visceral feel to it that really makes the character feel powerful. The character actions are a blend between combo abilities (similar to BDO), and 1 off actions that all have a variety of different cool downs. Character creation is deep, and well thought out with a lot of great presets to start from which allows a variety of good looking characters without a lot of time investment. If desired, more time can be spent to create something totally unique, or even possibly absurd. Ralph Pootawn comes to mind here. Templates can also be saved for later use, and the files can be provided to other players to load for their characters. I'll also not that characters don't start out looking like homeless drifters. Right from the beginning, they look at least respectable. The UI is very well done, but the translations are a work in progress. 90% of the time they will be enough to get by. There is an included auto run system that allows your character to automatically travel from one location to another, and it works exceptionally well most of the time. Often times the path it will take the character is inefficient to varying degrees. It tends to be wide on corners, and it often will walk you all the way around an area rather than straight through it. On the plus side, my character has yet to get stuck while auto running. I've only briefly used the taming system, but so far it seems interesting. All characters are able to tame almost any animal in the game, and then use it as a mount or a combat pet. I've managed to tame 5 different animals as mounts. This has proven very useful, as each mount has it's own stamina that is consumed while riding, but slowly regenerates when not in use.

DUSK isn't a bad game. It's just not nearly as "flawless" and "brilliant" as it's been claimed to be. While it's obvious where the game gets it's inspirations from, I would say it fails to deliver the same level of quality, creativity and gameplay than the 20 year-old games have that inspired it. It feels unpolished, clunky at times and poorly balanced. It also looks quite rough and i'm not talking about the low-fi aesthetics. Texture misalignment, ugly textures, and goofy looking models are what I mean. I will compliment the sound and music design though, it builds a thick atmosphere but I don't see the benefit in that considering it tries to be a fast paced 90's action shooter. The combat just feels so "off" that it doesn't produce the same adrenaline like actual 90's games did.  Let me elaborate on that. The combat is pretty clunky compared to the likes of Doom and Quake. Some enemies move around very sporadically and don't telegraph their attacks well, leading to some awkward battles and unavoidable damage at times. Enemy projectiles are fast as lightning too, this isn't that big a deal until you get into the 2nd episode where they throw a lot of enemies at you from high places that aren't easy to hit because of the way they dart around.   The bigger enemies can hit like a truck, dealing massive amounts of damage in a single projectile. In open spaces, running around and avoiding them isn't usually too bad but often the level design puts you in tighter spaces, or fills larger areas with a lot of obstacles to get stuck on. You can go from 100 health to 0 so fast you didn't even register what killed you. The high damage of enemy attacks is likely due to the poor enemy AI, it's pathetic pathfinding and simple behavior overall.   The devs, having failed to create challenging enemies, compensate for this by having them deal a lot of damage (on the harder modes that is, the normal and below difficulties have the enemies dealing lower amounts of damage, so low that it's so incredibly easy to walk through the game first playthrough.) The hardest mode just has enemies kill you in one hit. It's so bizarre to balance your difficulty like this. It's the laziest way to do so. It doesn't make the combat more challenging, it just causes you to quick-save more often.   Despite this, an experienced FPS gamer will have no trouble with the difficulty of the game. I played on the 4th level of difficulty in my first playthrough, after having felt the first 2 levels in Normal difficulty was way too easy. Enemies just don't do much to really threaten the player, most move slowly, they attack slowly, and can be killed in a single shot, with few exceptions. Most levels I didn't die once, the few moments of death I encountered were due to large amounts of enemies in hard to reach places. (Bosses are a joke, didn't die to any of them so far.)  I haven't finished the game yet but I probably will. Like I said in the first sentence of this review, the game isn't bad by any means. It's what you would expect a low budget indie game made by a guy or two to be. The praise and review scores this game got though, truly strange to see. I'm not sure why it's getting treated so positively when the game is underwhelming in it's combat design and overall gameplay. I can confidently say that if you skip buying this game, you aren't missing out on anything special.   It just doesn't deliver on the gameplay like it's hyped up to do. It fails to do anything truly new or special in the genre. It doesn't have the same level of quality than much older games do. It's level design, enemy design, weapon design and structure feels so derivative that it's not just a game that was inspired by Doom, it's a game that tries to be Doom but with 1/10th the talent behind it. I can actually imagine this game coming out in the late 90's as a poor "Doom clone".  Anyway that just about wraps it up. Again, not a bad game. If i could give this a real rating, i'd give it a 3 out of 5. Only worth playing if you are a die-hard Doom/Quake fan looking for something similar to play. Just keep your expectations low going into it. It really isn't mind blowing in any way, not that I expected it to be. 5 minute gameplay videos reveal exactly what you are gonna get here.   Side-Note: I'd really like to see this developer take on a pure horror game because I think that's what the game actually does best. Building a dark atmosphere that is actually fairly creepy at times. The ambient soundtrack is excellent too.

Castle Crashers is multiplayer sidescrolling beat-em-up. You can level up abilities and equip different pets and weapons in order to become more powerful and complete many different levels.  Breakdown:  Okay things:  -Solid multiplayer fun. It's decent fun to just load it up with your friends and play through a few levels. Not too much to say on this.  -Music is alright and atmospheric. It's usually fairly simple, but it sets a mood for whatever level you're in. It doesn't distract from the gameplay while still being significant enough to add to the experience. It's a hard thing to balance, and this game does a solid job on it. However, if you start paying too much attention to the music, you might realize it's fairly repetitive, and you might get annoyed, so I can't praise it too highly.  Slightly Bad things:  -Lots of items, characters, and pets are locked behind certain out of game things, mostly owning other games from this developer. It's not a huge deal, but it's slightly irksome that not all items are unlockable through the base game.  -Tries too hard to be funny. For example, there's a level where you traverse through the woods and encounter many animals who poop all over the place for no reason. It's just potty humor. It's not a huge deal, but I'd be lying if I said it didn't detract from my experience at all.  -In multiplayer games, one player can fall a bit behind and lose relevance. This game can just have a bit of a snowball effect. If one player does poorly in the first couple of levels, the other players will level up faster and be more powerful. This makes it so those players get most of the kills and experience in future levels, causing the player who did poorly early on to fall further and further behind. That said, the effect isn't that huge, and this game is too casual to care about it all that much, and it won't even be a problem in certain groups.  -Odd visual issues with the resolution. The game looked a bit off when I first opened it, so I set it to my computer's resolution, but that caused it to get much worse. I double checked my resolution, and it was exactly what I put in. I basically had to try other resolutions at random until one of them fit.  -Many interesting combos that just don't feel rewarding. The game has a lot of interesting combos and magic abilities, and it can be fun to try to use them creatively. But, after doing that, I just tried button mashing with only a little direction, and it seems to work just as well. So why does this game bother putting it all these mechanics if they don't even matter? As I mention later, this game is quite chaotic. So the problem here is that the game seems to have more mechanics than it needs to. The chaos just makes all these mechanics not feel meaningful in the slightest.  -Poorly designed UI. Just one example of this is when you want to get items, and it gives you a little summary of the stats of that item. However, this overview is usually partially covered up by the player portraits (gets worse the more players you have), and it requires some annoying finagling around to actually read the summary. (I previously had this under "bad things", but a friend informed me that you can hide the player portraits, making this more workable. It can still be annoying when you're picking up items in the middle of a level and want to keep track of all the players).  Bad things:  -Extremely chaotic and cluttered screen. There just tend to be so many things on the screen, it can be very hard to tell what's going on. This issue is exacerbated during boss fights. The bosses often take up so much of the screen. In one fight, I was fighting the minions while my friends were taking on the bigger boss, and then the boss stepped in front of me, and I could no longer see the fight I was having. Another example is a boss in which there is a ship who helps you out. Although it takes up about 1/3 of the screen, which isn't exactly helpful...especially because the boss itself also takes up about 1/3 the screen, leaving you very little to work with.  -Hitboxes very hard to deal with. The game is 3D but with 2D graphics, and the depth can be very hard to judge. I'll try to hit an enemy, but oops! I was standing 2 inches behind it, so I missed. This works the other way as well. Several bosses have attacks that take up almost the entire screen, so you have to rely on moving forwards and backwards to dodge it, but it can be really hard to judge that.  -Misc bad game design decisions. Several examples: A mini-boss who has a very fast long-range attack that does a lot of damage...and the attack isn't telegraphed at all. Also, a boss who revolves around a certain mechanic to beat that you might not even notice exists, unless you're paying attention to the background. And, as mentioned, the game is chaotic enough as it is, so you're probably paying attention to the boss and its attacks, rather than random background elements that don't seem to be impacting the fight.  -Poorly optimized. This game came out in 2012, and I played it on a new-ish computer that is mid-range in terms of power. And yet, I have consistent frame lag throughout the game, despite not having any other programs running that take up much CPU power. My friends also ran into this issue.  I don't just mean the game wasn't running as smoothly as it could've been. I mean the game occasionally slowed to a crawl, running at 1-3 FPS. This game has fairly simple graphics, and it's somewhat old, so I see no reason why it should run into slowdowns on my computer.  OVERALL RATING: 3.5/10 - Would not recommend buying.  The only reason I would ever recommend this game is if you are a huge fan of the genre, and are constantly looking for new games to pick up, and you enjoy them enough that even a mediocre one will satisfy you. Even then, this game isn't great in singleplayer, so I still wouldn't recommend unless you have several friends with similar taste as well.  For the rest of you, I can't recommend this game. The overall quality is quite low, and there are numerous major design flaws.

Another game that pretends at being old school while missing the point entirely. Hint: old-school games were not built around speedrunning. It's like Super Ghouls n' Ghosts if that game were stripped of all its charm and built around pixel-perfect timing with zero margin of error. In short, Volgarr the Viking is a game that is trying entirely too hard.  At its core, it is simplistic and unsatisfying. There's no weight in your attacks - enemies simply explode into blood mists when you strike them. It's not nearly half as cool as it sounds. The controls are tight and responsive, but a platforming section that was fun the first 3 times is not fun at all the 40th. Checkpoints are anethema. I was very surprised that I didn’t like [i]A Hat in Time[/i]. I went in anticipating an homage to 3D platformers like [i]Mario 64[/i], thanks in large part to the way the game sets itself up, but the whole experience quickly derails into an incoherent mess of ideas and gameplay styles, none of it executed particularly well. Really, it’s a mistake for the game to bait a [i]Mario[/i] comparison, because while it may be an impressive step up from that series’ early 3D entries, it absolutely pales in comparison to later iterations, especially the same year’s [i]Mario Odyssey[/i].  The big problem with this game is the way it swings wildly between half-baked level concepts, but honestly all of that would be okay if the platforming wasn’t floaty and unpolished. Ultimately, though, this game can’t even pull off one of [i]Mario Sunshine[/i]’s ‘platforming in a white void’ interludes without falling flat. This game doesn’t really feel like it wants to be a platformer, preferring to veer off course from dodgy jumps into the bizarre territory of drawn-out minigames and gimmicks that ensure that it never really fleshes out any individual mechanic past the preliminary stage.  That said, lots of people are going to like this. It has that simple, colourful art style that’s been popular since time immemorial, and its cutesy character design and absurdist world will go a long way for a lot of people. All I can say is that I don’t think this has the focus or execution to stand out amongst the oversaturated GameCube flashback market, and unless you’re absolutely foaming at the mouth for something to submerge yourself in and forget that you’re not a pre-teen anymore, I really don’t think [i]A Hat in Time[/i] is going to do much for you.

The characters are *a whole lot* too long-winded and irritating, but that’s the exception that proves the rule I guess.

This game has me really conflicted. On one hand, the concept is cool. On the other hand, it's poorly executed. Some songs are really good and catchy, while others are boring. Some levels have really cool designs that are really fun, while others are indistinguishable from other levels prior. The difficulty is good for some levels, but completely unfair in others. Most of the positives i've listed are mostly in the same levels together, while most of the negatives are in their own levels. Meaning that the good levels are very very good and the bad ones are very very bad. Now, I like to blame myself as much as the next guy; I want to just be bad at the game. if I'm just bad, that means I can grow better. If I can grow better, I can enjoy the game. The thing is, this game's "difficulty" isn't like Super Meat Boy or Touhou where the only thing holding you back is your own ability to beat the level. This game's difficulty comes from throwing random objects at you, killing you, and then hoping you remember the objects for next time. Imagine a Super Meat Boy level, but all the obstacles were invisible and as you slowly make your way through the level, every time you die to one of the invisible obstacles it becomes visible. So, EVENTUALLY, skill becomes a factor, but it isn't until you've died multiple times. That's what this game is. Nothing is choreographed well, you just have to guess where obstacles will come from and what they'll do. I got close to the end, but I decided 20 bucks for a 2 - 2 1/2 hour campaign that I hated myself playing wasn't worth the price and I stopped before I couldn't refund it.

This game is a huge disappointment. It doesn't know if it wants to be a wannabe-sim, or an arcade racer. Both the "gamer" and "simulation" steering modes feel awful to play with. Gamer steering feels so wrong, you can take a corner full speed and drift through it like you're playing Mario Kart.  Simulation steering was supposed to be the same as DiRT Rally, but it is not. It has been simplified to make it playable on a gamepad, but it ruins the experience for wheel. Out of these options, i think simulation steering with a gamepad is the best choice, even though it is infuriating to play with the wonky physics.  In landrush events, it's even worse. These are almost impossible to win when the cars handle so bad and the AI is actively trying to murder you.  Graphics in the game are average at best. The detail outside the tracks is very much lacking, and the textures aren't really mind-blowingly beautiful.   Still, my biggest complaint would be the tracks. They are pieced together from short, maybe 100m premade bits, built like a scalectrix track. Sometimes you might even find the same bit with only 3 corners back to back 3 times in a row, which makes the tracks incredibly boring and predictable. But then again, knowing exactly what ever track is going to be after racing on just 2, will help you compensate the terrible pacenotes.  Many of the pacenotes are plain wrong, and they don't seem to have calls such as "tightens into a" and "bad camber" at all, making it really difficult to drive without learning the track bits first.  If you want a casual DiRT game, play DiRT 3. Or the WRC series. This one is nowhere near as good as the older Colin McRae and DiRT titles used to be.

If you’re like me, and decided to jump on the DiRT series with DiRT Rally, then I am gonna have to disappoint you with the fact that DiRT 4 is not a worthy game to your collection. Ultimately trying to regain some of the fans they managed to get with fun accessibility of DiRT 3 with the brutality of DiRT Rally, but manages to complete neither and fail miserably in both.   Graphics - A very noticeable step down from DiRT Rally, both in the details of the cars and of the tracks as well. Hell, I’d even be bold enough to say that DiRT 3 looks better than DiRT 4 in a lot of places, making this area feel like it was just rushed.   Tracks - A interesting idea that was utterly butchered by the way they decided to execute it. I really liked the idea at first with the tracks being randomly generated, as for amazing as the tracks in DiRT Rally are, they do loose a bit of their undiscovered novelty after 223 hours of playtime, and the introduction of this would mean endless track combinations and makes the co-driver be more important.   But alas… That was not the case.  The tracks are incredibly bland, utilizing a tile system where you will end up seeing several of the same tiles in the same track, which just means that the inherent idea of randomness gets thrown out the window in a system that promised to fix set problem. And the general flatness of the tracks, there being no spectacular pieces like the hairpin and following straight next to the cliff on Anodou Farmakas, just to name a example, but I also think that it wouldn't be possible with this tile system anyhow.   Racing Ai - Wholefully inconsistent. You can set the Ai to one difficulty and consistently be leading them by 30+ seconds each track, only to turn it up a single difficulty level for them to dumpster you the other way around. There doesn’t feel like there is any form of curve here, but rather just walls that makes having fun on Champion an impossibility, unless you want a lot of stage retries or wishes to disable restarts and pray to god that you don’t crash.   Joyride - Has a bit of novelty to DiRT 3 in its style, but loses its charm quickly. There are only 4 or so tracks per discipline (A time attack where you can gain and lose time by pickups, and a smash attack akin to DiRT 3’s Gymkana), which become stale fast with the limited amount that there are.   Handling - Here, they also tried to appease both the hardcore and the rookie with a realistic and “GaMeR” handling, which honestly just feels like you are toggling a grip modifier in the background, and not doing that much else. Also it feels a lot more sluggish than the handling model they used in DiRT Rally, which makes me wonder why they didn’t just port that over and make a completely separate handling model for gamer, instead of making one that just butches both.   Conclusion - By trying to appease both the hardcore crowd and the casual one, they end up falling in both departments with a game that feels stretched out thin and unfinished. The track feature they marketed themselves with is bland and becomes predictable within a few tracks, the handling is poor and ultimately feels like a husk of both DiRT 3 and Rally. You could try and get it on sale for < €18 like I did, but even then it feels like I got robbed when considering what you end up losing in comparison to the prior titles in the series. So, even if you want to have a full collection of the DiRT games, you can skip 4 and still be able to sleep well at night.

I've been waiting for a game like this for a looong time (I'm a huge fan of games like Company of Heroes and Age of Empires), so I definitely fit into the developer's intended audience (just keep that in mind of you don't like those games).  It does feel like a medieval version of Company of Heroes: units are organized by squads, base building is there but minimal, skirmish involves taking objectives on the map to diminish enemy points, and there is even a retreat button for your squads. Some have bashed the game, saying the combat is boring, which I don't really understand since there is more to it than most RTS out there.  Units clash with really well done fight animations, archers are effective but cause friendly fire (so placement is important), cavalry devistatingly crash into enemy troops but are vulerable to spearmen and can't sustain combat well, and units can even hide in the environment (such as tall grass) for ambushes.   Visually the game is just great: trees sway in the wind, blood will mix with the river water, the unit and facial detail are fantastic for an RTS, and small details like villagers on fire fleeing burning buildings feels appropriately brutal.  I love the music in the game!  Definitely fits the theme and gets you in the mood for a skirmish match.  There are some cons though: - Voice acting is hit and miss in the campaign.  Some are great, some are atrocious. - I just wish there was more.  More maps, maybe another faction? Or a few more units that would increase the uniqueness of existing factions.   - While all 4 factions are different from one another, they tend to blend together more than those of a game such as Company of Heroes. - 10 squad pop limit is a bit small. I think I understand why, but more would have been nice.  Overall it's a quality game and I highly recommend it to those interested in the setting and/or genre.

This game has a lot of potential. I mean A LOT of potential. The graphics are cool, the soundtrack is amazing. The art direction is great, the stories are also pleasing. All of this deserves a job well done. However, the gameplay on the other hand is simply put very boring.   - First off, the fight engagement is annoying tbh. The fact that your squad can't move unless you retreat is quite frustrating. It may seem more realistic but gameplay-wise this slows everything down. The fights take their sweet time and don't end for quite a while. If fights were quicker maybe this wouldn't be that much of a problem.   -Second, the fight mechanics such as flanking and outnumbering are pointless. Yes, they give you an advantage but not much plus there are no visible effects which does not make it satisfying. I can still beat the enemy with more men why try and flank them? Which most of the time is quite hard to pull off btw.   -Third, archers and mounted units are ineffective. Mounted units are definititely useless they are way too fragile to do anything. Even when you charge retreat and charge again they are pointless. Use your 10 pop cap on something else (This is also another issue...) . Archers on the other hand are useful for destroying buildings from afar or getting rid of enemy ranged units yet that is their only use case. They do way too small damage in order to be useful against melee units. They can get in 2 or 3 shots max before they get charged. With a 10 pop limit I only use them as siege weapons and sometimes to counter ranged. Oh btw, if you block the enemy by engaging them with melee units and try to shoot them with your archers, most of the time you do more damage to your squad due to friendly fire. Don't think about any kind of strategy or sth like that. This again is probably a feature implemented for realism but it does not work in a game.   - Fourth, the 10 pop limit is very restricting and stops you from having epic battles. The 10 pop cap leaves you very few options to use as military units. Since the melee units on foot reign supreme in this game you are at a disadvantage if you don't use them and since you have 10 unit cap you can't really spare slots for other interesting units. In order to defend yourself properly from different routes, you either have to move your whole army around or divide it into groups of 3 or 2. And since archers and mounted units are useless you cant really have a group of 3 containing them because you are at a major disadvantage. So you spam your huskarls, spear guards and shield bearers and use them. Which makes the game very boring since these units act entirely in the same way except that one is better than the other. They are only different because of the unit triangle. Sure they have different abilities but these do not feel impactful at all. They do not offer any diversity. Their stats are also different apparently but there is no indication as to how different they are. The game just says high defense vs medium defense which gives you no clue as to how much of a difference that is. Anyways, I digress. All in all since the pop cap is not enough, the unviability of certain units stand out and you don't get to strategize.  Due to these features the fighting ends up being very dull, you just sit there and watch while you click on certain abilities of your squads periodically. There is this blob of warriors in the middle of the screen which you stare at mostly because there is nothing else to do. The base building and village manamegent is so easily and quickly done that you end up doing nothing. I generally don't like games that require micro but this game has none to the point where you have nothing to do. And even when you can handle the actionless minutes, the game does not offer any diversity in gameplay. You can't use different tactics or other units, you can't change your style of play. Even if you play with other clans which are essentialy reskins, they offer minimal variety. I say wait for sale or an update which can spice things up because at the moment, the game is just boring. I had such high hopes for the game too...  TL;DR  Amazing visuals and audio with an okay story. Boring gameplay, boring to the point that you will get sick of the amazing visuals and the audio in a couple of hours. Wait for an update or a sale to buy.

I wish I could recommend this game. A roguelike platformer inspired by Mega Man X really sounds like the dream, but alas, it is not.   The levels generated are very rarely interesting. The main issue is that most of the obstacles involve waiting a lot (moving platforms, falling blocks...) or moving very slowly (ice platforms). It affects the pacing a lot. This wouldn't be SO bad in itself as they are pretty standard mechanics in platformers, but what makes them unbearable is that they're not placed cleverly, and they usually come in huge chunks and are not combined with other obstacles to make for interesting emerging gameplay.   The bosses are well designed, they're all different from each other and they scale well. To me, that was the only interesting part of the game; the rest is not so bad at first, but it grows old pretty fast. I also appreciate the multiplayer, and tons of little details (getting bonuses if you finish a level under a certain time, having two playable characters, daily/weekly challenges), but it cannot make up for the boring level design.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]  The wolf is coming..  You like fairytailes? With a dark setting added to it? And somehow they all are using a magical item which turns them all into humans to hide their true form to the world? Hold my red apple, because you are in for a ride.   [h1]Analysis[/h1]  You are playing as Bigby Wolf, the big bad wolf. Now a sheriff of Fabletown where many other know characters live that you have heard about.   The game is a point and click game with some quick time scenarios, it also features lots of moral choices that can alter the story. Like many Telltale Games you can be outright polite, be quiet, don't care about anything and just be grumpy all the time, or something inbetween it all. Overall Bigby is quite a grumpy fellow so the choice is yours.  The game is split into five episodes, all delivering quality content in my opinion.  [h1]Verdict[/h1]  I belong to the herd that say that The Wolf Among Us is probably the best game Telltale ever made. I think the voice acting, the handling the story and the tension in the game was amazing. I'm glad that I bought this game on the same day episode 4 came out (iirc) because I was just yearning for more and more after playing it.

[h1]Almost Good, Utterly Generic[/h1]  While not a bad game by any stretch, Cave Story + is not especially exciting either. Bugs, blandness, and an overall lack of polish make this one hard to recommend..  The story has to do with some unexplained war, an 'ancient evil awakens', and amnesia. This unfolds through a series of little cut scenes sprinkled throughout the game. As the player progress more is revealed through character dialogue and a few events, such as before and after a boss battle. There were a few moments that were kind of amusing, but the story here is pretty weak, and often generic.  Game wise the action is never more than decent. Shoot, jump, swim, and navigate your way through a small but diverse set of locations, find some secrets, and really just explore. Most weapons are standard; blaster with three levels of power,Super Mario style bouncing fireballs, missiles, charge beam, etc. Upgradable versions help keep things balanced, such as a sword that unleashes a rapidly striking ghost, or the aforementioned charge beam. A few weapons are actually pretty cool, if a bit overpowered for the most part, which helps cut some of the monotony down.  Speaking of monotony, this game tends to be really tedious. Backtracking and fetch quests take up the bulk of the player's time, along with sometimes painfully slow dialogue boxes. You can't skip the dialogue, which can get really frustrating because most f it is forgettable, boring, or just bad, and if you’ve messed up and need to restart you have to sit through those big chunks of dialogue all over again. It can be really frustrating.  There is a lot of okay level design, but it is, mostly very plain and uninspired. You get big empty chasms with platforms, or narrow hallways with platforms. I felt a strong sense of atmosphere from the floating island of talking dogs. For whatever faults I felt playing this game, this sense of atmosphere and presentation gave me a sense of nostalgia, particularly for the old days of Super Nintendo and Sega Genesis era gaming. Points to the designer for accomplishing this, it's just a shame more wasn't done with it. What we get is a lot of potential, but not a lot of very exciting execution.  Controls are okay, but not especially tight with a game pad, which is a shame because some of what is needed to win will take precision that just isn't there without a keyboard. Using both a PS3 controller and an Xbox One controller, I found that often the left and right movements would stall or not respond properly. For some of the trickier extra stages, like Blood Stained Sanctuary, I found myself depending heavily on the arrow keys despite spending a lot my time trying to make it work on the d-pad.  The soundtracks are pretty good, very reminiscent of 16bit era platforming games, with three versions of the game's score to choose from in the options menu. Graphical options are pretty sparse, but this isn't really a bad thing as the game's styles really are pretty good at helping set the tone.  Overall this looks and behaves like a classic 16bit era game, but with only really basic level and quest design elements. Visually this is mediocre, but serviceable. Some might say that it is important to take the age of the game into consideration, but SNES games were doing a lot of what's in this game long before this came out, and they were doing it better. Still, this is an impressive effort despite its lackluster parts.  It is worth mentioning that some bugs linger, and since this game is not longer supported by the developers you will have to take it “AS IS”. This includes the buggy controls, crashes, a broken achievement (with a user made fix), and other quirks.  [b]Pros:[/b] [list]     [*]Atmosphere     [*]Music is decent [/list]  [b]Cons:[/b] [list]     [*]Annoying dialogue     [*]Heavy backtracking     [*]Bland story     [*]Lame level design     [*]Tedious game play     [*]Boring graphics     [*]Unreliable controls     [*]Unfixed bugs     [*]Not developer supported     [*]Doesn't always play nice with D-pads [/list]  [b]Verdict: 4/10[/b]  I've played this game several times over the years, and every time the words 'boring' and 'overrated' came to mind. This isn’t a bad game, but it's just too generic and frustratingly tedious to be all that exciting.

I am a long time Total War and RTS gamer. I've been disappointed in Warhammer 1 and 2 with the exception of the modding community. The game is a watered down version of all the other TW games to date. Three Kingdoms has recaptured some of this.   Folks will proclaim the 'magic' or the lore is amazing, but the fighting itself is very minimal. I have been in countless 'wars' where the AI will remain with their armies just out of range of me and never attack even if they declared war (This was a feature in Atilla as well). I once chased the entire Orc horde back to the mountain pass without fighting them. They refused to stand and fight in Total War. Granted, they will attack an undefended settlement if they have the chance. Never if it is a fair fight. You have to chase them till they either relent, a spy slows them, or their last city is destroyed. I once saw the High Elves abandon their island and sail away as my horde of armies landed.   Things that were removed heavily from these games, besides the cowardly AI, is a Navy, actual diplomacy, and unit formations. Chaos could be knocking on the door of your neighbor but they won't trade with you for an extra $70 a turn. In Shogun 2, rival units would even negotiate to trade with you as they (also) like money during a massive war.   A naval battle would be nice. There is the Man O' War expansion in Warhammer. We have pirates and Black Arks (which are generally useless), but they will happily land at a nearby island to settle a naval battle. Black Arks can bombard, but can't land at cities or raid them?   Heroes are great till they aren't. You will engage a Hero who is a higher level and surround him with 3000 angry Dwarves with axes and do 0 damage to them. The hero will be happy as can be in this situation. Just push Fast Forward to speed up the battle and get a beer in hopes you win.   Map designs are lazy and uninspired. Do you want to use terrain to your advantage? What terrain? Every map is flat, open and maybe has a rock or a shrub. You can only frontally assault a city with walls. You can't attack on 2 fronts, spread out or make the defenders nervous. City Towers can shoot the entire distance of the map. So in a siege battle you will unpause and immediately be under fire even though you have siege engines yourself. Stopping a siege tower or battering ram is difficult as you don't have siege engines on the wall, can't equip everyone with fire arrows or have your towers shoot at the siege equipment (can't control them at all actually).   Units can't change formations such as shield wall, pikes, frenzy or others manually. They will engage their special abilities if they want too. So if you want to hold your ground there is no option. Archers have to be made individually instead of choosing the arrow design.   Magic. It is fun for a minute then it is meh. Oh, and never give your mage a horse and Auto-resolve. It is an easy way to get your mage dead. Apparently the AI plan is the Mage charges immediately. It is frustrating.   City design is boring. Check out Three Kingdoms. There are more JUST Farm buildings than buildings in ALL of Warhammer Total War. All your cities and provinces will be the same save a legendary building here or there.   City defense without walls used to be you with a militia actually defending the city. So you can hide in alleyways, use chokepoints and make the attackers pay for assaulting your small city. In Total War the militia defending the town will ride out for an hour and stand in the middle of a boring wide open map and wait on the overwhelming force to kill the crap out of them. A mod will allow you have walls in all cities because this 'feature' is stupid.   Allies are generally useless. You can request them to join you on a point; they won't join you on their own.   Trespassing is annoying. Diplomacy to demand that unit marching through your area leave isn't in the game. In other Total Wars; if you walked into a territory without asking it could cause war to immediately be declared. It meant you had to negotiate or go around some areas to continue your fights instead of just walking through.   Folks who have read this far will likely decry the things added to the game or how they don't want to use unit formations, but they like Magic or flying. You aren't listening to yourself. We want our games to be us against the world. We want to use our tools and designs instead of just paper v rock v scissors and hope our unit wins in the scrum. We want options, not less options.   TL;DR: No Navy, limited diplomacy, AI runs away from fights, magic is meh, heroes are stupid, maps are open fields, and city designs are the same. Get Shogun 2: Fall of the Samurai for the best Total War since Empire. Hopefully Three Kingdoms will right the ship.

Iconoclasts is a compelling game from start to finish. The game-play itself is quite enjoyable with puzzles and exploration being main tenants of the game's design. The combat takes many cues from the classic Metroids and has a great sense of its own personal style. There are also many memorable boss fights that are challenging, but never feel unfair. Iconoclasts really nails just the right amount of difficulty.  Where Iconoclasts really excels is the storyline. It is absolutely brilliant. All the characters are well-fleshed out. The main themes really hit home. It is perfectly shown. Iconoclast really ran with the metroidvania formula, tossed in more story elements, and took it home.  Grade-A meat. Ten outta ten.

I cannot recommend this game enough. The gameplay is great, but what impressed me the most was the narrative. The story actually gets quite dark as the narrative progresses. If you like mature, hard-hitting stories, you should not miss out on this game. Indeed, the thoroughly conceived characters, storytelling, and worldbuilding elevate this work to a level that few games achieve. It's mind-boggling that this was all created by a single person. Large teams struggle to create this overall level of detail, quality, and depth. I took my time, but it took me about 14 hours to get through the game, including some additional exploration and such. I can see the average playthrough being about 10-12 hours (longer if you want to be a completionist or challenge the higher difficulties), and it's well worth the money. The launch price of $19.99 is a bargain for what you get.

I haven't finished Iconoclasts, so maybe I will come back and change this review but at this point I am probably going to stop playing because I'm tired of all the little annoying things that this game keeps throwing at me.    There are a few things this game does very well, the world building is well done and intriguing, some spots have poor pacing but I keep wondering what is going on and why, which is great.  The graphics are very well done in their chosen style.   The sound effects are well utilized and well synched and at least one or two of the tracks are well done.    This game is at its best when it tries to be fun and when it tries to show you it's world.  This game is at its worst when it wants to drag you through aspects of its gameplay because it feels like it has a duty to show it to you.    Now here's all the little annoyances in case anyone wants to read through all of them.   Iconoclasts acts like it's trying to be a metroidvania but it can't let go of the player and give them any freedom which is a core concept of the genre. Building on that, the items you could backtrack for are near useless anyway and the crafting system is somehow underutilezed even though the only thing you collect is crafting elements.   Those enhancements you craft are practically useless and dissapear after a few hits, when I forgot about them I suffered no ill effects. The combat gets stale quick.  It needs probably twice as many weapons or abilities or something. The only interesting mechanics is the electric tether ride thing and that's fun, but that's it.   Most boss fights are puzzle fights that are terrible at telegraphing what you're supposed to do.   The menu interface is terrible, why can't I hover over my items to see what they do, or for quest items find out where I'm supposed to go or who to talk to. The characters are one-note, if they have a note at all... The protagonist somehow has less personality then a regular silent protagonist and I'm not sure how they did that.  The other characters are only a shade more interesting, if only smelly was a personality aspect, one character would be two-note! If you made it this far, congratulations, your life must be as boring as mine! Last but not least, You're an action platformer, YOU DON'T NEED A STEALTH BASED BOSS!  LEAVE STEALTH TO THE STEALTH GAMES! I don't hate this game, but I am really annoyed by it because it could be so much better with a little better direction.

All around, Bomber Crew is a solid game with adorable, voxel graphics, and reminds me a lot of FTL.

I was surprised by how slowly this game given the fact that the game is nothing more than a single 3D room, simulated computer parts that you can interact with, an a simulated internet through which you receive orders from customers and and place simulated orders for parts.
